There arc two motions before the House of þÿCommons the object of both of which is to convey a censure upon, or vote a want of confidence in, the Government. The one has its origin on the Liberal, the other on the Conservative, side of the House. The elder, in point of date, is due to Mr Roebuck, and would condemn not only the present but the late Government, for the

abuses disclosed before the Sebastopol Committee. The younger, but more important, of the two has been placed on the paper by Sir Edward Bulwer Lytton, and directly censures the Government for participation in the sentiments of Lord John Russell þÿ as avowed in his too notorious and melancholy speech on the þÿAustro Russian propositions for an illusory, and therefore dishonourable, peace. Mr. þÿRoebuck motion s sinks into insignificance compared with that of Sir Bulwer Lytton. The mismanagement in the Crimea, disgraceful as it was, has been to a large extent remedied ; but nothing can remedy the evil inflicted on the Cabinet and the country by the speech of Lord John Russell, except his retirement from the Ministry. Lord Palmerston may, perhaps, find means to avert a Parliamentary censure ; but if he do he will be fortunate and clever indeed, if he attain that object without the sacrifice of his blundering colleague. An attempt is to be made to screen Lord John Russell by the publication of further correspondence relative to the Conference at Vienna, tending to prove that M Drouyn de Lhuys, who, like his Lordship, was bamboozled, bewildered, tricked, and made a dupe of by the adroit Count Buol and other Austrian influences, did not for that cause lose the favour of his Imperial master, but fell from power on account of a difference on another question. But all this is nothing to the point. Lord John þÿRussel con- s duct is to bo ju i ;od by his recent speech ; and by that speech he sh ws himself utterly unfit to

be the member of a Ministry pledged to carry on the war with energy and vigour, and whose boundon duty it. is to spare no exertion to secure a victory. Lord John Russell must resign. There is no alternative, except it be the dismissal from office of the whole Administration. þÿ lllus London News.

THE ATTACK ON THE REDAN. All the advantage we gained by the assault on the lledan on the 18th ult. was the capture of the Cemetery, and even that we hail nearly abandoned, owing to the timidity of one of our Generals. As the men in the Cemetery and houses suffered severely from the þÿenemy sfire, and the soldiers in the latter were not able to withdraw till nightfall, one of the Generals of Division gave orders to abandon it On the following morning an officer of Engineers, Lieutenant Donnelly, heard, to his extreme surprise, that the position for which he had paid so dearly was not in our possession. He appreciated its value þÿ lie saw that the Russians had not yet advanced to reoccupy it. With the utmost seal and energy he set to work among the officers in the trenches, and begged and borrowed some thirty men, with whom he crept down into the Cemetery, just before the flag of truce was hoisted As soon as the armistice begau the Russians flocked down to the Cemetery, which they supposed to he undefended ; but, to their great surprise, they found our thirty men posted there as sentries, who warned them hack, and in the evening the partv was strengthened, and the English are dow constructing most valuable works and batteries there, in spite of a heavy fire which occasions them considerable loss Lord Raglan is said to have found fault with General Eyre for losing so many men, but the latter observed that he had done what he was ordered, and that he had taken the Cemetery There can be no doubt but that our troops could

have got into the town in the rear of the Redan from the houses on the 18th, had they been strong enough to advance from the Cemetery. Whether they could have maintained themselves there, under the fire of forts, ships, and batteries,

V '& U '1 'JL A T '1 is another question. It is now shrewdly suspected, however, that inside the Redan, behind those outward and visible walls of earth, there is another very strong þÿwork a kind of star fort of earth with sunken batteries and it is certain that þÿ inside the Malakoff works there are several lines of battery which have never be?u unmasked The enemy have probably constructed large funnel-shaped pits 'behind these works, into which shells roll and burst, as such a þÿ þÿdodge was found in the Mumelon. Inside the latter work were splendid bombproofs for the men to retire into when our fire became hot. They were large pits with ten feet of earth, and beams of wood across them, and were capable of holding a strong body of men In one some new sacks marked with the broad arrow and B. O were found, in which were packets of cartridges ready for use. Where did these sacks come from ? It is almost as strange as the English bread found at Tehorgoun. A NEW LOAN FOR TURKEY A convention has been signed in London by the Ministers of England, France, and Turkey, and sent to Constantinople for the exchange of ratifications, by which England and F ranee are to guarantee a loan of five millions sterling, to he raised on behalf of the Turkish Government. The loan will be effected in London, and will bear interest at 4 per cent, per annum. The money cannot be raised until the ratifications of the convention have been exchanged and au Act of Parliament has passed to enable the British Government to give its guarantee to this stock. It is, of course, stipulated and intended that the whole amount raised shall be strictly devoted by Turkey to the purposes of the war, and wc trust that very stringent conditions will be introduced iuto the arrangements to provide against the notorious abuses of the Turkish Treasury, which have proved so injurious to the credit of the Ottoman Porte. It also remains to be seen what is the nature of the security tendered by the Turkish Government, and what are the means proposed for the redemption of the debt. These particulars are not yet before us, but. they will, of course, be made known to Parliament in detail upon the introduction of the bill It is not expected that the money will be raised before the month of August. þÿ London Times. -« ooo «« LAUNCH OF THE þÿ PERSIA þÿ

From the " London Times. ,r It is rather a remarkable revelation to be made without any reserve or misgiving, that there exists in the Cabinet which is wholly responsible for the continuance of the war a Minister of great consideration who thinks it unnecessary. That is the fact. Not deterred by his rebuff the other ovening, Mr. Gibson last night renewed his efforts to probe the great mystery of the Vienna negotiations. This is not the first time, nor the second time, nor even the third time 1 that, after a due bombardment of questions, an attempt has been made to assault the rampart of official reserve, and get at the reason why Lord John left Vienna so abruptly, and how it came to pass that the Austrian Minister, and others as well informed, confidently stated that Lord John was ready to make peace, as some said, on any terms ; at least, on terms that Austria would agree to. It comes out that the English and French Plenipotentiaries were agreed, and that they returned home to recommend to their Governments the acceptance of the Austrian proposition ; that M- Drouyn de Lhuys, on finding he had not the concurrence of his Government, resigned ; that this want of concurrence was owing, not to the independent opinion of the French Emperor and his advisers, but to the dissent of the British Government; and that, notwithstanding that dissent and the consequent retirement of the French Plenipotentiary, Lord John Russel has thought it best to devour his differences in silence, and to assist his colleagues in carrying on a

war which he believes to be wholly gratuitous, and involving the nation in the guilt of causeless bloodshed. All this was rumoured, not only here, but throughout Europe. Reasons were even assigned. Some said that Lord John had been seduced by the hearty and good-natured tone of the Russian Plenipotentiary; others, that he had learned more than he chose to tell, including some vision of danger from some quarter or other to the country ; in fact, that he had þÿ seen a þÿ þÿwolf, and that his very silence was portentous. It was then stated very confidently that when he resumed his place in the Cabinet he made such a case that he won over several of his colleagues to his view of the subject ; that the Cabinet was thereupon divided into a peace party and a war party; that the war party carried the day, and that Lord John Russell, conceiving that lie would be nobody and would do no good out of the Cabinet, resolved to forget his advice and the whole chapter of his unsuccessful diplomacy, and hold on with Lord Palmerston. We ventured to intimate ourselves that the case was very much as we have stated it. Yet, when the opportunity occurred, and the special invitation came, to give Parliament a full account of the failure of the Conferences, and Lord John Ru þÿsell own s part in it, his Lordship flew off into some historical declamation about the immense power, dangerous position, and overweening ambition of Russia, the general effect of which was that he was quite as much heart and soul in the war

as any of his colleagues. As might be expected, we came off ourselves rather ill. We were charged with having imagined a dissension between Lord John and his colleagues, with having fabricated a peace party, all out of spite either to Lord John, or to somebody, or to everybody. Indeed, we have seldom had so much abuse as for this one false

a ir ut <s> i Aprils and malicious statement þÿ viz., that Lord John Russell had come back from Vienna with an Austrian proposition for peace, and had strongly urged his colleagues to agree to it, but that they had refused. After a silence of we know' not bow many weeks, so long and so profound that really Lord John aud his Conferences had almost come to be forgotten in the gravity of passing events, all of a sudden last night, on Mr. þÿGibson mere s interrogatory, Lord John made a clean breast, telling everything with the simpiicity of a child. It was perfectly true that lie had acquiesced in the Austrian proposition, and expressed an opinion in private to the Austrian Minister that it afforded a means of carrying out the third point as satisfactory to the interests of Europe as to the honour of Russia. It was quite true that M. Drouyn he Lhuys had agreed with him. It was true remained the sam opinion still, and to tins day thinks we are lavishing our blood and our treasure without any necessity for it. It is also true that there was good precedent for withdrawing in such a case þÿ the case, viz., of a decided difference of opinion with the Cabinet on tbo most important question, not of the day, but of the century. Was there ever anything more ingenuous ? If the position in which his Lordship now stands he not quite accountable on the common notions of consistency, constitutional propriety, and even personal honour, still there can he no doubt as to the farts of the case. We now know all about it. Mr. Gibson has

broken the mystery, and captured the fortress, by the simple expedient of walking right into it. On the former occasion Lord John was evidently in no humour to give satisfaction, and preferred to raise a cloud of dust about Russian aggressions, or anything whatever. On this occasion lie has been so prompt, so explicit, and so natural as even to suggest the idea, which, of course, has no foundation in fact, that he was not only prepared for the question, but had even contrived it, in his fear that more delay would occur, and that Parliament mark : þÿ would separate before he had had the opportunity of informing the world that he stood in precisely the same position as M. Drouyn de Lhuys, excepting only that the Frenchman had retired from office, and the Englishman had not. Well, this is, to say the least, a very odd story. There are not many men in England, we had said in the world, who could stand up and tell it with Lord John þÿRussell s matchless composure. þÿ Evil he to him that thinks þÿevil. No doubt Lord John is an honourable man ; so long as he is satisfied he is acting for the best, and doing his country more by hanging þÿout anywhere else, and service by staying in the Cabinet than þÿ knocking about among the various nondescript Oppositions, his Lordship must be considered the best judge of his own | conduct. At the same time, we could

a syllable to save our own humble selves . þÿ from the charge of lying and slandering, profusely heaped upon us when we i spoke of the peace and war party in the Cabinet, and said that Lord John had brought and recommended overtures of peace from Vienna. There is, too, anoj ther unfortunate mallapropos in th« ti ne which his Lordship has selected tor his tardy confession. It is much the same as what happened at Christmas. On that occasion, after keeping to himself, or at least from the world, for threequarters of a yea., Ids objections to the i imperfect state of the War Ministry, and June 28.

his distrust of the hands in which it was placed, he found himself at last obliged to speak out at the very moment when the Government was on the eve of dissolution under the storm of public disgust at the mismanagement of the war. As nothing can he more disagreeable to a generous nation than to desert friends in the hour of petil and disaster, so his Lordship was truly unfortunate in having put off a good intention till it assumed the appearance of that equivocal act. In the present instance, it so happens that we have had, till just now, a run of successes, or something like it, ever since Lord John returned from Vienna ; so decided, indeed, at first, that certainly a proposition to make peace with Russia on the Austrian terms would have sounded very ridiculous. The restored health and increased numbers of the allied armies, the arrival of the Sardinian Contingent, the improved condition of the camp and the hospitals, the coni stant repulse of t he Russian sorties, the capture of the Mamelon, the occupation of the Sea of Azoff, and the prospect of cutting off the Russian supplies þÿ all kept up a state of confidence, in which it would have been an act of uncommon courage, to explain what Lord John did last night. The scene has now unhappily changed. VVe are experiencing the dark side of war. There is, therefore, now no rashness, no courage, in the confession of peaceful wishes, and of an inward dissatisfaction with the war. Most heartily do we condole with Lord John

on the delay which has timed his explanation at so ungracious an hour. But, as truth is always desirable, and better late than never, we will still beg to thank his Lordship for a statement which the British public, and, indeed, all Europe, had certainly some right to he in possession of, and which is also due to our own vindication. . !>.

We were acquainted with the deceased from our youth, and have always admired his urbanity, and felt pleasure in his society ; therefore do we testify to his qualities as a christian, a countryman, and a friend. He arrived at St. Thomas in ill health in December last, and found the writer of this inadequate tribute to his memory surrounded with grief, and ho adraiustered much to our consolation ; since then we have been called away to this Island. The object of this notice, when circumstances would allow, was always seen in the House of God, and when out of it deported himself iu such a way as to win the esteem of every acquaintance, at home and abroad. SPEECH OF THE EMPEROR The Emperor of the French opened the Legislative Assembly on the 2d July, þÿ lows : and, in so doing, spoke as fol- " Messieurs les þÿSenateurs Messieurs les Deputes: The diplomatic negotiations commenced during the course of our last session already made vou foresee that I should he obliged to call you together when they came to a termination. Unhappily the Conferences of Vienna have failed in procuring peace, and I come again to appeal to the patriotism of the country and to your own. Were we wanting in moderation in settling the conditions 1 I do not fear to examine the question before you. One year already had passed since the commencement of the war, and already France and England had saved Turkey, gained two battles, forced Russia to evacuate the Principalities, and to exhaust her forces in the defence of the Crimea. We had, moreover, in our favour the adhesion of Austria, and the moral approbation of the rest of Europe. In that situation the Cabinet of Vienna asked us if we would consent to treat upon bases vaguely formulated. Before our successes a refusal on our part seemed natural. Was it not to lie supposed, forsooth, that the demands of France and England would increase in proportion to the greatness of the struggle and of the sacrifices already made. Well, France and England did not turn 1heir advantage to account, or even make the most of the rights given to them by previous treaties, so much had they at heart to facilitate peace and to give an

unchallengeable proof of their moderation. Wc restricted ourselves to ask, in the interests of Germany, the free navigation of the Danube, and a breakwater against the Russian flood which congreat river. We demanded, in the in- tinually obstructed the mouths of that the rank which is its due. Faith in the terests of Austria and of Germany, a better constitution for the Danubian Prin-

cipalities, that they might serve as a barrier against these repeated invasions of tin- N irtli. We demanded, in the interests v humanity and of justice, the sum guarantees for the Christians of every confession under the exclusive proiectiou of tile Sultan. In the inter 'sis of the Porte, as well as in those of Europe, we demanded that Russia should limit to a reasonable degree, sufficient to shield her against any attack, the number of her ships in the Black Sea, a number which she could only maintain with an aggressive object. Well, all these propositions, which I may call magnanimous from their disinterestedness, and which were approved in principle by Austria, by Prussia, and by Russia herself, have evaporated in the

" Russia, who had consented, in theory, to put an end to her preponderance in the Black Sea, has refused every limitation ot her naval forces, and we have still to wait for Austria to fulfil her engagements, which consisted in rendering our treaty of alliance offensive and defensive if the negotiations failed. Austria, it is true, proposed to us to guarantee with her by treaty the independence of Turkey, and to consider for the future as a casus belli an increase of the number of Russian ships of war exceeding that before the commencement of hostilities. To accept such a sition was impossible, for it in no propo- manner bound Russia ; and, on the contrary, we should apparently have sanctioned her preponderance in the Black Sea by treaty. The war had to follow its course. and " The admirable devotion of navy will, I trust, soon lead to a the army happy result. It is for you to provide me with the means to continue the snuggle. I had resolved t" go and place myself in the midst of that valiant army, where the presence ol the Sovereign could not have failed to produce a happy influence; and a witness ot the heroic efforts of our soldiers, I should have been proud to lead them; hut serious questions agitated

From the " London Times." If anything could increase the disgust and indignation justly caused in this country and throughout t he world by the details of the Ilango Massacre, it would he the tone in which General De Berg has undertaken to justify the atrocities committed on that occasion by the troops forming part of the army under his command. It is true that the statement originally made by the seaman John Brown has turned out to he in one respect incorrect, for the number of persons killed on the spot by the Russians was happily not quite so large as this man supposed, who saw them shot down before his eyes, and was himself shortly afterwards wounded and left for dead in the boat. Nor can we wonder that under these circumstances of horror, deprived of all his comrades, the man believed that every one of them had perished. But, with this exception, we are compelled to state our conviction that on ail (lie other points of his counter-statement General De Berg's assertions are false; and, though we are dealing with a heartless and treacherous enemy, it is not without reluctance that we make this charge against an officer holding the rank of Aide-de-Camp-General of llis Majesty the Emperor of Ali. the Russias, an officer, moreover, whose family were in former times well known and esteemed in this country.

As we shall presently show, there are several points in this narrative which are not only wholly at variance with the evidence of John Brown, hut with the facts known to the whole crew of the Cossack, and reported by Captain Fanshawe himself. There is, however, one preliminary consideration which must strike eveiv one who reads this melancholy story. Lieutenant Geneste and Dr. Easton are happily -'ill alive. The Russian Government cannot he dev >id of shame as not to f I tin- imparlance of removing, if possible, tins foul blot upon their flag and their military reputation. They have it in their power to produce unimpeachable evidence on the whole case, in the form of depositions made by the officers who were taken prisoners; and, to make it apparent that such depositions are not taken uadei constraint, they might he received by the Rev. Mr. Law at St. Petersburg. This expedient is so obvious that it must have occurred to them ; yet no such depositions are produced. They therefore come into court as men who suppress the most material witnesses against themselves, and, as far as General De Berg's account of the transaction goes, it rests almost entirely on secondary evidence. General I)n Berg endeavours, in the first place, to shift the question by a general statement that English vessels occasionally hoist Russian colours, and that on the 26th of May a cutter from some unknown ship had landed Willi a little white flag near the village of Twermimie, and had set fire to some huts

and boats there. With reference to this last occurrence we are without inl'orma tion, but General De Berg cannot he ignorant that the practice of hoisting different colours on a cruise is a practice sanctioned hy the immemorial usage of all maritime nations. It can, however, in this case deceive no one, for no one at. this time imagines that the Russians will themselves dare to show their flag in any sea beyond the range of their batteries. The Russian commander then goes on to argue that this cutter came in "with a hostile and hy no means truce-like character;" that no flag of truce was seen; that loaded arms were found on hoard the boat, including three muskets, which were fired in the struggle; and that the crew were provided with 360 cartridges and a chest of incendiary articles, which were taken hy the enemy. As to the object of the cutter in going into llatigo, it is admitted hy General De Berg himself that his own countrymen, the Finnish prisoners on hoard the boat, were either killed or wounded; and the fact that these prisoners were on hoard is conclusive evidence that no hostile demonstration was intended. Indeed, it leaves no doubt as to the true object of the boat's mission. Yet, with this fact before him, General De Berg affects to throw doubt on the veracity that ' Lieutenant Gem - i e pretends that of a British officer, and says " he was sent with a flag of truce to "give up the crew of so e merchant- " men," þÿ evidently intending to dispute the assertion, though it wn , supported

not only hy Lieutenant Gene-ie, hut by Captain Fansh awe and hy Admiral Dundas. As for the flag of truce itself, we have a precise declaration from Captain Fanshawe that "it was first displayed when "about half way Loin the ship to the " shoi e, and ; . . a. iii a mile from " still in (consequently " shore sight of the ship). No blank wlien the boat was " guns or muskets were fired, hut the " flag, tchich teas on a boarding pike, was,

" hy Lieutenant Geneste's orders, kept " clear, in a good position to be seen." General De Berg will perhaps admit, in cooler moments, that this particular and authentic declaration is of more weight than the alleged report of his outposts, which report, however, is not produced. We h ave an equally positive declaration that the muskets in the bottom of the boat were not loaded ; and as to the story of the cartridges and combustibles, it i> altogether incredible. Does General De Berg, or will any one else, suppose that 17 British seamen could have found themselves in such a position, with loaded arms in their possession and have allowed themselves to he shot down without inflicting the smallest loss upon their assailants t At one moment General De Berg says that three muskets were discharged in " the struggle;" at another that " the affair lasted only a moment," though " seven men were ' killed, four wounded, and the rest " made prisoners." þÿ a fact which is itself conclusive evidence" of the brutal ferocity of this massacre. General De Berg, however, does not express the slightest regret or compunction for this wanton execution. Iledoes not attempt to explain why no warning was given to the boat, if the Russian outposts did not choose her to land, or why the party were not captured, as they might easily have been l>v the overwhelming force that lay in wait for them. claration that " the responsibility of the He contents himself with a jaunty de- " whole affair rests with the irregularity " with which missions of this sort are

"made." As far as the strict inquiry instituted l>y Admiral Dundas proves anything, it proves that the mission of this flag of truce was conducted in the form used on such occasions, with the sole exception that the stewards of the mess were permitted to go in the cutter, þÿ a slight deviation which certainly does not prove the hostile character of the expedition. If any doubts were entertained hy the Russians of the intention of the boat's crew, or of the purposes to which flags of truce might he turned hy their adversaries, they would have been quite justified in warning off the cutter, and compelling her to return to the ship. But there is something more than an "irregularity" in converting the reception of a flag of truce into an ambuscade for t he murder of a party of unarmed men, and in attempting to justify an action which has excited the indignation and horror of the civilized world. The observations which the Journal de St. Petersbourg has added to this correspondence are a mere attempt to throw upon us a portion of the obloquv lliev have so justly deserved themselves. If it appeared to the Russian Government that flags of truce had been used bv their enemies for unfair purposes, it was competent to that Government to decline to receive them. But we have not forgotten that their very first act of hostility was to fire on a flag of truce at Odessa, that the same disgraceful act lias been repeated at Hango under circumstances of cold-blooded cruelty, which it is now attempted to palliate hy
the grossest misstatements and aspersions upon an act dictated hy motives of forbearance and courtesy to the Russians themselves.

The Country Schools. We publish to-day iu our columns a portion of a Communication, proposing ameudments to the Law regarding the Country Schools, from the pen of a member of the School Commission. The subject is ably handled by our correspondent in his introductory remarks, and his communication will, we think, bo perused with interest by our readers. The Country School Law is, wo are of opinion, a very imperfect one. Full time, however, was given to the public for the interchange of opinion on the subject, by the publication of the draft some months before the session of the Colonial Council, which advised its adoption. That lamentable apathy to public matters, in this, as in other cases, prevented the free discussion of those defects in the law, which must have been quite as apparent then as now. The subject is again before us ; and wc trust this communication will elicit the free opinion of all competent to form one on the matter. " In the discussion of public subjects" says the memorable Daniel O'Connei.l, " truth is a duty and not a crime." This, we fear, requires to bo impressed on the minds of our fellow-constituents, and when onec fully impressed, wo have no fear then of hasty and imperfect legislation. Our censorship is not of that severe kind which forbids the expression of truth when eonlined within orderly limits; none, therefore, need be afraid to exchange opinions on public subjects. Wc shall be happy to insert any communications which may treat on subjects concerning the

public welfare : and it may be well to state here, for the information of those not aware of the fact, that communications cost nothing for insertion, but, on the contrary, are thankfully received The only right we reserve to ourselves is that of refusing insertion of an article, when not of sufli cient interest

The Weather, Ac. Til e occurrences since our last are not many Those who have been crying out loudly for "Rain ! Rain ! Rain !" have had the element of Aquarius to their heart's content. On Sunday evening the Weather presented a very inauspicious and threatening appearance, indicating a heavy fall of Rain, which proved correct. Rctween 8 and 9 o'clock at night it commenced to rain in good earnest, and continued pouring with " hail stone" drops þÿ and with scarcely any cessation þÿ until next morning, when the clouds assumed a much milder aspect ; it however continued drizzling until yesterday afternoon As a natural consequence the streets and roads have been, from the heavy and continuous fall of water, more or less cut up and otherwise injured, some of the latter, wc are told, being rendered impassable. In town, we have little to record, except it may be that Princes Street exhibited

more the semblance of a river than a path for pedestrians. Among the shipping in port, we regret to learn that the Danish brig Najaden, Captain Kalsen, met with an accident ; sho was struck on the mast by the lightning, which shivered it, and caused damage to some portions of the iron work about same. The electric fluid then ran down the mast, found its way into the cabin, where the Captain was sitting at a table, þÿ he having barely escaped its influence, þÿ and disappeared out of the stern glass-windows, smashing the panes in its rapid course. From

leading from Mount Welcome Avenue to Spring Gut has suffered dreadfully, and will require considerable repairs ; also that a Horse belonging to " Beeston Hill" estate was struck dead by the lightning. Several trees, learn, we were likewise struck and destroyed. These are all the incidents and accidents that have come to our knowledge connected with the Weather. Some say there was a shock of Earthquake just before the first severe peal of thunder, but we did not experience it. We have not learnt how the Weather has treated our friends at West End. From the Sister Islands we await intelligence also.

The Emperor of the French litis added to his just fame l»y the utterance of a manly address to the Senate, in which lie depicts in truthful, though gentle phrase, the treacherous double dealing of Austria. Holding that double-dealing Sovereing to be bound by the terms of treaties, the French Emperor almost avows þÿ certainly intimates þÿ that he expects no performance of these obligations. Napoleon has the sense to see what our Ministers cannot or will not see, or have not the manliness to avow, ; that the Austrian will do nothing that is not simply scllish, or that is wise, or just, or honourable. The French Emperor's speech has touched the hearts of the people of this country as well as those of the people of France, and already is there intrigue at work to prevent the due effect of his manly and sensible address. The King of the Belgians, who, from being a sensible and plain-dealing monarch, litis, since bis son's marriage with the sister of the Austrian Emperor, lowered himself to the degrading employment of an Austrian agent, lias hastily arrived in England. Is court influence to be used here to save and serve the Austrian ? Let us hope that it will be used in vain. Our alliance with the French Emperor is worth twenty alliances with the Austrian

Imperial tricksters, and must not be for one moment weakened even though the Austrian Court should be mad with rage, or sinking with fear, at the French ex posurc of Austrian knavery; for knavery it is, and nothing else. If financial embarrassments alone caused, as it is pre tended they do, the reduction of the Austrian army, that reduction could he safely and honestly made on the side of Switzerland and of France, the first of which is friendly, and the second of which is in alliance with Austria, instead ot being made on the side of Russia, with which, if Austrian faith and Austrian treaties were worth anything, Aus tria ought now to he actually at war. flic Austrians' object in making it there is to enable the Czar to despatch more troops to the Crimea. French and English blood pays for the Austrian Emperor's treachery. I'lie people ot England are too inert respecting this war, which drains their blood and empties their pockets. They trust too much to untrustworthy events. The Ministers have done nothing to jus tify confidence in them. They make every act a mystery, antl therefore tliey justly excite suspicion, for mysteriousness and sincerity are very rarely capa hie of combination. The people should defend tli eir tiueen and themselves, against influences which may betray the interests of both. þÿ London Paper. \ mcrica. From the " London Times." INDIA. BOMBAY, June 10. We have news at last from Central Asia, in the shape of a communication to the Delhi Gazette from its correspondent at Bokhara. The letter is said to have suffered severely on the journey from the precautions taken to conceal it, all transmission of news being strictly forbidden by the King under pain of death. Among other parts thus rendered illegible was the date, which, however, is approximately arrived at by the knowledge that the caravan which brought it left Bokhara about the middle of April. It states that a collision has taken place between the Russians and the troops of the Khan of Khiva, in which the latter were worsted with considerable loss. Hitherto the Russians are represented to have been careful to avoid hostilities with the Khiva people, preferring to make their way by negotiation, and their troops remained in cantonments on the Khan's frontier. Here their convoys were attacked by a body of Alamans, who had previously plundered several villages in Persian Khorasan, and large herds of sheep and cattle were carried off. Thus active measures were, it would appear, forced upon the Russians, and the result was the engagement I have mentioned, and which we may suppose will be followed by an advance upon Khiva. At Kokan it is said that the Russians had been less successful, and that the troops of the Khan have as yet held out against them, but that their numbers and influence are steadily increasing. Meanwhile Persia, on her side, is in

arms, though apparently not yet as the avowed ally of the Czar. That portion of her army which is operating against Khiva from the south had sustained a defeat at Meru, and fallen back, but, having been reinforced by fresh troops, had again advanced into the Khan's territory. A Persian force has also, as we learn from Cabul, appeared before Herat, the chief of which place, receiving no succour from Cabul, has at last been compelled to place himself under the protection of the Shah. The King of Bokhara is reported and we may well believe with truth to be finding his position an unpleasant one, and to be watching with considerable anxiety the absorption by the <reat northern Power of his neighbours of Khiva and Kokan. Among them is one of a Mr. Thompson, which his friends, among whom are some of the leading merchants of the country, are urging Mr. Marcy to take up, and which illustrates the entire absence of responsible government in the island of Cuba. Mr. Thompson had been in business as a merchant, and an agent also for the management of Spanish estates, at Sagua la Grande, for many years, and had accumulated a lucrative business, as well as a handsome property, both of which were regarded with envious eyes by less successful rivals, lie enjoyed also the favour and friendship of all the Government officials residing in the place; so much so that for the last five years the prosecuting attorney had been a constant guest at his board, and the Lieutenant-Governor had been a frequent guest with him, often for weeks together. The magnitude of his commercial relations, his success in accumulating property, and all his interests, prompted to a strict neutrality in politics, which his friends all say he rigidly observed. About two years ago, at the request of the United States' Consul for that district, he consented to accept an appointment as sub-consul or commercial agent, in the place of an Englishman, whose removal became ne-

cessary in consequence of a regulation by the department at Washington that no foreigner should be appointed to ofthe office, and took possession accepted fice in a consular bureau. He cember or January last, and 1hen re- continued to occupy this office till De- j moved into an adjoining house in the same street, and constructed exactly in the same manner as the old house, There lie occupied the room upon the ground-floor corresponding with that which he had occupied in the old house, situation with that which it corresponding and erected the shield in a filled before". I he district attorney also followed him to his new abode, and continued a guest as before, and be lived on in apparently cordial and friendly relations with the authorities until, in March last, the police came to him and directed him to remove the shield in 15 minutes. lie refused, and thereupon they took it down themselves, took him prisoner, sent him to the Havannali as a felon, destroyed his native business by stamping him with Government odium, and interrupted the foreign correspondence which required his personal presence. been guilty. Probably no other lately which the Cuban authorities have case equals this in hardship. þÿ þÿHarrier, June 24 þÿSir, 1 have the honor to inform you that the boats of this ship destroyed forty-seven ships belonging to the enemy, varying from 700 tons to 200 tons, ou the nights of the 23rd and 24tli instant. Unhesitating abject obedience, is the keystone of all its power, and it. cannot become the propagandist of liberal principles, or the fomentor of resistance to legitimate authority anywhere, without teaching its own people a lesson that would shake its throne. The Packet ! The packet Vigilant arrived here precisely at 9 þÿo clock on Friday night with our European Mail, which was issued from the Post-office early next, morning. Sir Wim.iam Moi.esworth þÿ according to a statement iu the London Times þÿ has succeeded Lord .John Russell in the British Cabinet as Secretary of State for the Colonial Department In the House of Commons, the Turkish Loan (£5,000,000) was brought on by Lord Palmerston, who moved the preliminary resolution, sanctioning the guarantee which the British Government proposed to give for the payment of the interest on this loan. Turkey, he observed, had made noble efforts, and won much honor in the war with Russia It was therefore no disgrace to that country to find its resources insufficient for its expenditure. Last year a loan was raised, from which about three millions was realized, hut now five millions additional was required. After explaining the motives which induced the Governments of England and France to offer their joint guarantee to facilitate this loan, the noble lord adverted to the prospects of ultimate payment. Towards the interest cf the new loan the surplus income from the Egyptian tribute, amounting to £65,000 a year, would he specially appropriated, and in addition the whole revenue of Turkey would be pledged for the i

liquidation of the debt. The guaranteeing Governments had taken further measures to ensure that the amount borrowed should he entirely expended for purposes of war. The resolution gave rise to a discussion, which lasted until midnight, and which had, as a result, all but the overthrow of the Ministry þÿ the Government escaping by only a majority of three. þÿ And this disreputable sortie of the united friends of þÿRussia, says the London Observer, þÿ was defeated only by a majority of three, by the chance presence of so many honest men, who had not left town, or who happened to be there to listen to the patriotic appeal of Lord Palmerston, and to vote against this latest of the Russian attempts to cajole and disunite us from our Allies and from each other. þÿ There never was a more perilous experiment attempted, even for the basest purposes of faction. Had it succeeded for a moment., an appeal to the full House of Commons against a dis-

creditable surprise, would probably have set mat ters right again. If it had not, then an appeal to the people most, assuredly would. þÿ If it be right to supply the Turks witli men, it is right to supply them with money. We have not even done this. M e only engaged to pledge our credit þÿ in conjunction with France þÿ in order to enable Turkey to borrow five millions upon terms less onerous than she borrowed three millions some time back. For this pledge of out credit to this limited extent, Turkey pledged her best revenues, and is, moreover, a country as yet unstained by repudiation. And it is on this pal try issue that a combination of the House ol Commons þÿ and such a þÿcombination has attempt ed to break through our Treaty engagements, and to peril the Alliance to which we are þÿpledged. Great preparations were being made in England to receive the remains of the late Field Marshal Lord Raglan. The Carudoc arrived at Malta on the 10th June, witli the body of the noble Lord. The vessel, it is said, was paint cd black in every part, everything denoting the deepest mourning. On her arrival the Union Jack was hoisted half mast high, and every demonstration of mourning made. The Caradoi proceeded the same day with the body to Eng land, in ediarge of Commander Derrimak, who had ever been in close attendance on his Lord ship during the time he was in the East, and on his promotion for his personal gallantry at Alma he was kept in command of the Caradoc at. Lord þÿRaoi.an s particular request. The mortal

remains of the late Commauder-in-Chief were expected to arrive at Bristol about the end of July. Prince Albert, the Earl of Cardigan, the Duke of Cambridge, Sir df. Lacy Evans, and a large number of the nobility, were to meet the body either at Bristol or at Badminton, where, according to the custom of the house ol Beaufort, it will lie in state iu the great hall for three days. Nothing important from the Crimea or Bailie of a later date has reached us beyond the ex tracts published in our last. The popularity of General þÿI elissier begins to decline. It is said that lie cannot agree with his brother þÿofficers that he is hot-headed and rash, that he is continually wrangling with General Bosqlf.t, and that, should he fail iu (ho next movement, he will fall disgraced. It was rumoured in Paris that a combined attack on Sebastopol by land and by sea would shortly take place. One hundred vessels and 40,000 men were to he engaged in this assault, while from the land side the assault would he vigour ously followed up the same instant Of course, this movement of the naval force presupposes that means have born taken or can be taken to force an entrance into the harbour, despite the obstacles which the sunken Russian vessels mav present. Rumours have prevailed, we are told by a Liverpool contemporary, þÿ to the effect t hat. the Russian ascendancy over Austria, in consequence of the recent misunderstanding of that power with France and England, had become so great that we may look for a speedy alliance between It us

sia and the two great Germanic þÿStates DISTRESSING CONDITION OF RUSSIA The most recent accounts from Russia allude to the collapse of several important national and commercial undertakings, owing to the want of funds or raw materials. PROSPECTS OF TIIE SIEGE Some little time must elapse before anything decisive can occur. Both French and English are working incessantly on the right ; but the þÿenemy works s do not allow of our opening the trenches by day þÿ it is only at night that our workmen can act. But at this season of the year the nights arc very short, and then it has happened that the Moon has been up. THE FIRST SHOT AT C KONST ADT. The Commandcr-in-Chief tried the range of a 32-pounder guu, which had been slung in a peculiar manner, at an angle of 45 degrees, in one of the wood-boats captured a few days ago. The boat was moored across the stern of the Flag-ship, and three or four shots fired; the fall of the first in the water was eagerly watched for, but it took so long a time before it fell that it was given up, but in a few seconds exclamations of astonishment burst forth as a small column of spray rose in the air at a distance of more than 5,000 yards, or over three miles ; the shot took exactly thirty-one seconds for its flight. The boat was then ttnved a little nearer the shore, opposite, one of the new earthen batteries, near the þÿgovernor house, s and a couple of shots fired to ascertain if they were within range. Both shots went a long way over the battery, which immediately returned an ineffectual fire with mortars that, would not carry the distance. These are perhaps the first shots from an enemy that ever alighted on the island of Cronstadt About an hour before dusk a small boat was seen creeping along the north shore towards St. Petersburg ; two gunboats were sent to stop it, and returned about elevem p. m. with it in tow. It contained three fishermen, who were trying to take three or four kegs of sprats to market ; after being examined and cautioned they were allowed to go away ; but this will show you with what vigilance the blockade is enforced ; within twelve miles of the capital of the empire,
and five of its strongest fortresses, not a boat even so largo as a Thames wherry can float upon the waters within our sight, and we have the complete command of all.

The short notice allowed to Denmark does not admit of her devoting tho necessary time to this important question, more particularly as at this moment Denmark is in a difficult arising from involve her in a war with Russia. To acquiesce in tho American demands would bring with it the sacrifices of thousands of pounds sterling for the benefit of other States, who, properly speaking, bear the whole burden ot these dues, while America seldom contributes more than $200 in a year to them Denmark is just at this moment least of all preprepared to make such a sacrifice as this. I cannot help looking on þÿAmerica s giving this notice at this time as hard treatment, by no means provoked by Denmark, for many have been the instances in which the Danish Government has remitted these dues to American merchants, contrary to all right, and solely in the hope of preserving the amicable relations of the two countries undisturbed. There the children attend school from their 6th (or if the parents prefer from their 7th) year until they have attained their 13th year; from the commencement of the harvest all schooling ceases for four weeks and the rest of the summer, chi 1eren over 10 years only attend school twice a week ; furthermore parents and masters all have a right to keep back from school children over 10 years during the sowing season in spring and autumn for seven weeks. Now, not only agriculture but also the intelligence of the rural population in Denmark is at as high a standard as both are low in this colony. In order to obtain a system of instruction by which we may be enabled to train the children of our rural population to become good and honest men and to teach them such knowledge and information as is necessary to make them useful citizens of the state, at the same time paying due regard to the wants of agriculture, and forming the special rules in just conformity with other enactments given for the labourers, l believe that a law for the country-schools ought to be founded on the following principal points : 1. Children are to attend school from their 6th to their lltli year. Parents have a right to demand the instruction continued until the Pith year on paying a reasonable remuneration. 2. The instruction is to lie given in the 5 first working days of the week, in

the forenoon as well as in the afternoon. 3. The children are to he divided in two classes, each to receive instruction separately, the one class attending school in the forenoon the other in the afternoon. 4. The principal branches of instruction are religion, reading, writing, arithmetic, singing and for the girls also sewing. 5. When a child has leanrt to read distinctly and is able to form ciphers and letters it is to he removed to the upper-class. The instruction ought to lie so that the children under ordinary circumstances may leave the lowest class when 1) years old. 6. Parents have a right to keep their children, who have entered the upperclass and are past 10 years away from school during the 5 first months of the year for the purpose of employing them to agricultural labour. E uropea n. From the London Times, August 15, 1855. A wearied, and it must be said a disappointed Parliament, was yesterday prorogued with the dull formality of n Royal Commission. Up to the very last moment the anxious Premier expected either from the North or the East the news that was to gild the closing session ; and, so long had hope been deferred, that it had yielded at least to misgivings. So utter was the blank, so little was there to show fot the labours and the enormous sacrifices of the Legislature, that when Sir De Lacy Evans arose to insist on a more searching and unreserved application of our national resources to t lie prosecution

of the war. Unit Majesty's Government seemed to lie at his mercy for any rebuke he might choose to administer. Hut while he was speaking the telegraph was already at work, and, but for those national jealousies which impede even the electric fluid at every capital and frontier, we should already have j learnt the utter destruction of the second Russian stronghold in the Baltic. Sweaborg has been almost utterly destroyed. A few shattered earthworks and batteries are all that survive of a mighty link in that chain of fortresses prepared for the conquest of Europe. It is impossible not to remark on the fatality which has permitted a zealous session to pass without receiving the tidings already on their way. The Roman poet laid his hero under the spell, þÿ At nuni/uatti regno , out optatu luce fruatur, sed cudut ante diem. That certainly has been the fate of this session; but when Ministers and Com- manders have toiled all their lives, and sunk heartbroken in the hour of reverse, though their cause was finally to prosper, Lord Palmerston has no great reason to complain It is but an imaginary disappointment. The | papers that take the þÿQueen s peech down to the country, and can report no more than Her Majesty's confident hopes and undaunted resolution, will now convey the news of Sweaborg destroyed We shall not be suspected of any idle or vindictive triumph tit a blow which doubtless involves much human suffering. We rejoice because we believe ourselves to be so much nearer secu-

rity and peace. Whether Russia will admit the moral argument of the defeat, or will await the successive destruction of all her strongholds, this event brings us nearer the day when Europe will be relieved from the incubus of Russian domination. Sweaborg cannot, indeed, be classed with Cronstadt for strength or Sebastopol for importance. Its defences are not of the same character as those which protect the mouth of the Neva. The approach is by channels of sufficient depth and width, but through granite rocks everywhere covered with batteries. As to the value set bv the Russians on the place, on the one liaud, it appears they took advantage of the winter to convey to (Tonstadt the few vessels of war seen last venr at Sweaborg; and, on the other hand, they have employed the interval in strengthening to the utmost the fortifications which have just been so summarily destroyed It was said a few months ago that, having let slip the opportunity of last year, we should find Sweaborg impregnable. It appears, however, that with a proper disposition of the fleet, and by keeping a proper distance, we have disposed of this threat, and shown that wood can sometimes beat granite. I.ct us hope that when a boast has been proved idle in one place it may in another, According to the programme, the mortar-vessels and the gunboats were to commence the bombardment at two miles distance, and the liners were only to come iri to finish the work If this is the arrangement which has been so signally successful, it augurs well for

the operation of the flotilla, promised by Sir ('iiaui.es Wood, in the grander sphere of the Neva, or wherever else it is to bo employed. from the scanty particulars that have reached us, it appears that the bombardment lasted about 15 hours, so that du-

3 tf © Hi <D 'X 3L A T U t 3 ring the whole of that time the allied fleets remained in position more or less within gunshot distance of the Russian batteries ; yet our loss is said to be trifling in men, and nothing whatever in material, not a ship or a boat sunk or disabled. In so large an amount of damage inflicted on the enemy and so little suffered by the allies may be seen the result of that close calculation which will probably be our best game in this war. Doubtless, more glory is to be won by dashing enterprises, done with small means by one mastermind; but, where the command is divided, the power immense, the risk great, and the defence in propoition. nothing should be risked, and nothing need be risked. Success is ours if we only have patience to use sure, though perhaps slow, means. This most welcome intelligence need not blind our eyes to the importance of the topics in Sir 1). We have at this moment not far from a hundred thousand good British soldiets in various parts of the world where there is no immediate need for their present numbers India ought to contribute something to the war in return for the 40,000 British soldiers withdrawn from our wants at home, and some regiments of irregular cavalry are precisely what we should most require in the case of an advance into the interior of the Crimea. At all events, the employment of that force at the Cape would liberate for the

Crimea someof the seasoned British battalions now thrown away in doing þÿwatchmen duly s against the Caflies With a larger military force we might attempt more enterprises, such as those in the Sea of Azof!, and that whose triumphant result we have this day to communicate from the Gulf of Finland. The actual successes of this year have been of a chiefly naval character. That is quite in accordance with the earliest anticipations of the war, when it was assumed that the immense armies and impenetrable territories of Russia must give her the advantage on the land. Latterly, however, the Fabian policy she has pursued of leaving the open sea, hiding her fleets deep in her harbours, and sinking them, if necessary, to block up the ports made for their reception, has turned the attention of the world rather too exclusively to siege and other land operations. Hence fleets have fallen into discredit as a useless pageantry of war, and doubtless the want of craft hot ter adapted for t he purpose has favoured this impression. Vet it is from the sea that the greatest blows must lie shuck against Russia, and in this pail of the work it will evidently be our honour to take the lead. As there was no military force worth notice engaged in the attack on Sweaborg, we conclude that the work has been done by the fleet, which contains a large preponderance of British vessels, ll this happy intelligence has come just too late for the Royal Speech and Lord þÿI almerston s valedictory address to the Commons, it is happily in

time for the þÿQueen s visit to Baris Indeed, on the very day, and almost the very hour, that Her Majesty is making the round of the Boulevards, the actual despatches brought by the Belicun yesterday morning to Daritsic will probably be placed in the hands of the Parisian newspaper readers. We are sure that our gallant allies will feel the happy omen, and welcome with their usual chivalry the illustrious lady who, on the very first
visit of peace ever paid by an English sovereign to Paris, comes also the bearer of the brilliant success that has crowned our united arms.

The Scandinavian Kingdoms. þÿ A correspondent of the Times , writing from Copenhagen, strongly urges on the English Government the advisability of showing sympathy for the political struggles and national feelings of the people of the Scandinavian States. þÿ Taking the three Scandinavian States together, it may bo safely affirmed that the national spirit is strongly anil decidedly anti-Russian. Luckily, the people of the North possess other elements of strength, which are to the spirit of nationality what a healthy physique is to the soul. They are not effete or falling into decrepitude, hut hardy, industrious, and progressive. They are more numerous and more wealthy than they were half I a century ago, aud they have had full experience of the evils that spring from division. In Denmark the national party is engaged in a struggle þÿ to be final and decisive þÿ likely to retain the popular constitution against the pressure put on the Government by Germany. In Sweden and Norway the question of a Scandinavian þÿ þÿunity is being agitated with increased þÿenergy. THE CONSTITUTIONAL STRUGGLE IN HANOVER. The first step taken by the new Hanoverian Ministry is one which will not tail to awaken the indignation of the whole kingdom. In an evil hour the King had been induced by the small Court party by whom he is exclusively surrounded to throw himself into their arms, and upset the existing liberal constitution, against the advice of the late moderate Cabinet, aud in direct op-

position to the wishes of tho people. A Royal proclamation was published on the lstinst., dissolving the Second Chamber of the Estates of the Kingdom ; and the next step will of course he to convoke a new Chamber, based upon the limited franchise of the former elective law. The country is completely taken by surprise. The Hanoverians, who have always been conspicuous for their loyalty to the family of the reigning Guclphs, are startled at the position they are placed in, of being obliged, in self-defence, to offer a steady but universal opposition, in order to preserve the dignity and independence of the kingdom. This opposition will no doubt be confined for the present to the legitimate steps guaranteed to them by the provisions of the constitution ; hut aud people already put their heads together þÿ ask, each with blank countenance, in knots, If these constitutional means fail, which they inevitably þÿ j will, what next r Emigration of Latter-dav Saints from þÿLivkrpooi.. Marine Intelligence. The English barque Lord Raglan, 277 tons, Captain Edwin Mc'Leon, left I)einerara on (lie 8tli inst., in search of freight. C II O L E R A ! ! \N i have the astounding report that Asiatic Cholera has re-appeared at St Thomas ! An official communication from that Island states that one confirmed case had occurred, and that Cholera does exist, while subsequent private letters assure us that such is really not the case tt ll us " there is a general report here of Cho- other documents of the same type (private) lera ; a woman has died, and the Doctors declare it a case of confirmed Asiatic Cholera /" There is still, however, a doubt, and we arc inclined to give our Sister Islaud the benefit of that doubt. Nevertheless, while hoping for the best let us prepare against the worst. Need we remind our readers of 1853-51, when that deadly foe dealt devastation throughout the length and breadth ot St. Thomas and St. Johns, sweeping off some two thousand in the former and one thousand in the latter Island. 'Twore unnecessary to recur to the foreign þÿIslands Barbados lost 20,000 of its inhabitants, Grenada 5,000 ; St. Kitts, St. Lucia, St. \ incent, and Trinidad shared a similar tatc þÿ we speak not of Jamaica, for there Cholera has become a resident. During that momentous crisis we were mercifully and miraculously preserved from a visitation of that dread scourge. Whether the fatal Epidemic does or does not exist iu our immediate neighbourhood 'he benefit of the doubt " Hope for the best, - we have already recorded our verdict, giving prepare for the worst'1'' þÿ let us, then, look around and see that our house is in order, Hope has
"ft told a flattering tale ; therefore we repeat

SV 0 Ut 4» 1 2£ A T It 3 that much infinite credit belongs to our authorities for the fore-haud and wise precautionary measures they have adopted. Without breaking the subject we may here state that we learn 5 days quarantine will be enforced on all vessels arriving from St. Thomas, and no passengers or luggage from that place will be allowed to land here, until further instructions. We opine that the advocates of non-quarantine would be aghast on rising some fine morning to learn that Cholera had been introduced into St. Croix. In Prussia and other parts of Europe the strictest discipline was used against the enemy, and the coasts even guarded, yet still ho entered the camp. This is, however, no criterion for us, as we have already reaped the benefits of a steady quarantine. Besides, the authorities hold themselves blameless by the rigid adoption of this rule however much þÿ commerce or private interest may suffer ; the sacrifice of human life is more for bye-and-bye þÿ none can with justice say " why was so and so not done." To conclude, we would suggest merely by way of preventive to householders, þÿ tenants, tipes., to keep their yards and around their premises free of all food that the implacable monster may feed upon. We are indeed happy to observe the gang busily engaged cleaning the streets, and removing away all unnecessary accumulations. Remember, remember the past. The following Recipe for Cholera, prepared by a gentleman in America, and used in upwards of 4,000 cases, all of which were restored, may not

prove unavailing should we become the unfortunate subjects of the fell destroyer : þÿ " One ounce Ciunainon ; one ounce Cloves ; one ounce Ginger ; one ounce Nutmeg, pounded well together, aud add half ounce of Cayenne Pepper ; infuse the whole in a quart of best Brandy. When mixed to be well shaken, then left to settle. Afterwards it will be fit for immediate use. When a person is attacked with Cholera, put iu a tumbler half full of hot water 3 or 4 lumps of refined sugar, and pour in a tabic spoon-full of the mixture quite clear. Never disturb the sediment- -give it to the patient as hot as he or she can take it ; and should the symptoms not abate, repeat the dose within au hour ; but this is seldom required ; put the patient to bed between þÿblankets the cramps will soon subside, and a full circulation and profuse perspiration will follow. Nothing more is required. By way of drink use warm rice-water ; Tea and Coffee to be avoided."

One sees plenty of miniature young ladies with basque waist and flounces, dress hats, and tinv watches, promenading the streets or attending juvenile parties : but, alas ! a little girl is a rarity þÿ one who will play baby-house and live a life-lime in n few hours, making day and night succeed each other with astonishing rapidity, a fifteen minutes' recess at school affording plenty of time for weeks of play-house life: one to whom a neat plain ginghnm dress and sunbonnet is the perfection of school dress, sunbonnets that will not be injured if they are wet in river or brook, and apron strings enough to bring home any quantity of nuts from the woods, in lieu of baskets; good strong shoes that will come off with ease on a warm summer's day, when the cool brook tempts the warm little feet to have themselves in its waters instead of delicate gaiters, which shrinks from such rude treatment. " Well I it is to be hoped the race of little girls will not become utterly extinct. There must tie some ' wasting their sweetness upon the desert air,' for surely they bloom not in our cities, and but rarely in our villages. " At an age when little girls used to be dressing dolls, we now see them decked in all their finery, parading street, and flirting with young students Where on earth are the mothers of these precious flirts ! Are they willing to allow such folly ? " Then as to dress: why, little miss must now be dressed as richly as mama ; and the

wonder is, how will she be able to outvie her present splendor when she 'comes out.' But in this go-head age, some new inventions will enable her to accomplish her desires. " As there are no little girls, so there will be no young ladies ; for when miss leaves school she is engaged, soon marries, and takes her place in the ranks of American matrons. How will she fill her place ? for how or when has she found time to prepare for life's duties. Wonder if it would tie a good plan to turn over a new leaf, begin with them in season, and see if it is impossible to have again darling little creatures, full of life and glee, who can run and jump without fear of tearing flounces, and finally have a set of healthy young ladies, upon whom the sun has been allowed to shine, arid active exercise in the open air bestowed an abundant supply of life and energy.

A Dirtier Hand Stii.l þÿ Dr. Wall once at a dinner party, very unwisely persisted in playing with a cork in such a manner as displayed a hand long divorced from the lavatory. One guest happened to express his surprise to another, and in too loud a whisper exclaimed "Heavens! what a dirty hand!" The Doctor overheard this, and turning sharply around said "Sir, I'll bet you a guinea there is a dirtier hand in the company." þÿ " Done" replied the first, sure of winning. Necessity is the Mother op Invention. þÿ During the celebration of the glorious fourth at Mokelumne Hill, it was found impossible to procure a cannon for the firing of salutes, but an inventive genius attached to the Union Hotel obviated the difficulty by adopting, as a substitute, a lot of quicksilver flasks, which were loaded with powder, buried in the ground endwise, and then touched off. Each of them burst into a thousand pieces, but the fragments were prevented from flying into the air, or from doing any injury, by the tight packing of earth about them. The explosions were deafning þÿ said to be almost equal to the report of a twelve pounder.

The Annales d'Hygiene, of Paris, has published an article pointing out the danger arising from packing snuff in lead, as the damp in the snuff' acting on the lead oxidises it, and forms a soluble salt of a poisonous nature. The use of lead envelops has therefore been discontinued.

Under the impression that the besieged would probably for the future keep a good lookout for demonstrations of this nature, the French, not many days since, made the same signal, and accompanied it with the roll of drums in the trenches towards the front, and words of command, given in a loud tone. I have been enthusiastic and joyful as any one after a victory ; hut also confess that even then the sight of a field of battle lias not only struck me with horror, but even turned me sick ; and now that I am advanced in life, I cannot understand any more than 1 could at fifteen years of age, how beings, who call themselves reasonable, and who have so much foresight, can employ this short existence, not in loving and aiding each other, and passing through it as easily as possible þÿ hut, on the contrary, in endeavouring to destroy each other, as if Time did not himself do this with sufficient rapidity ! what I thought at fifteen years of age, I still think ; " war, with the pain of death which society
draws upon itself, are hut organised barbarisms, an inheritance of the savage state, disguised or ornamented by ingenious institutions and false eloquence." þÿ Louis Bonaparte.

WEALTH. It is a beautiful remark of Lord Bacon, "Seek not proud wealth ; hut such as thou mayest get justly, use soberly, distribute cheerfully, and leave contentedly." And says the late William Wirt þÿ a name that will long he illustrious in American history þÿ " Excessive wealth is neither glory nor happiness. The cold and sordid wretch who thinks only of himself þÿ who draws his head within his shell, and never puts it out hut for the purpose of lucre and ostentation þÿ who looks upon his fellow-creatures, not only without sympathy, hut with arrogance and insolence, as if they were made to he his vassals, and he to he their lord; as if they were made for no other purpose than to pamper his avarice, or to contribute to his aggrandizement þÿ such a man may he rich, hut trust me, he never can he happy, nor virtuous, nor great. There is in a fortune a golden mean, which is the appropriate region of virtue and intelligence. He content with that; and if the horn of plenty overflow, let its droppings fall upon your fellow-men þÿ let them fall like the droppings of honey in the wilderness, to cheer the faint and weary pilgrim."

an i: ok hoi ntr ii. Fourteen miles to the east of Placerville stood one of those immense trees known in California as the Fremont, or Sugar Pine. In circumference, two feet from the ground, it measured twentynine feet, or nine feet four inches in diameter. It was chopped off" only two feet from the ground, as there was no apparent diminution in size for fitly feet upward. As many men as could work around it chopped it off in two days. It made in all two hundred and sixty-five thousand shingles ! At twelve dollars per thousand, the price they brought at the stump, we have no less a sum than $3180 for shingles alone, beside shakes, rails, and fence-posts. The entire length of the tree was two hundred and thirty feet.

THE AGRICULTURAL REPORTER A gentleman has sent us tho following extract taken from þÿ I be St. Croix Agricultural Reporter, No. 9, for July þÿ1853 þÿ a publication j which we regret to say has ceased to exist for the sheer want of due encouragement þÿ which we deem appropriate, and may be re-perused with a degree of interest : þÿ þÿ Wo have to regret much that a certain degree of apathy has been more or less shown by tho Members of tho Agricultural Society to contribute their quota towards filling tho columns of i the Reporter. It may be remembered by those who closely scrutinize the pages of our publication, that a great similarity has prevailed in tho subjects which the various writers have touched upon. But this was natural, as the object to be gained by the Society and the Reporter was, to aid Agriculture and to disseminate J þÿmen sopinions on its various branches. How-

ever, we do not think it out of place to moot a question of the greatest importance to ourselves, as well as the whole community, premising that the larger the crops are the more beneficial they | are that same community. On this point we believe every one will acquiesce. We are about to touch upon a most delicate subject ; one that has been discussed by persons of all occupations and of course discussed pro et con. We a lude to | that formidable subject of the þÿ yearly þÿcontract. We do not intend to enter into all the arguments prospect of more. Our planters have nearly j that have been raised as to its advantages or disadvantages. We profess to be as thoroughly philanthropic as the most frequent attendant of weekly 1 experience which the votaries of that Exeter Hall ; but we must insist upon having an institution have not ; and what we wish to impress upon our readers is the great and vital importance, for the future welfare of this colony, that this contract should be fairly carried out. We say þÿ þÿfairly, for who that reads these pages, does not know all the disagreemens and heartburnings that take place during the months of August and September ! And if these contracts were fairly made, that is, if the planters were to remain passive and 1 quietly allow our labouring population to seek employment, instead of being sought for, would it not be advantageous to all ? We have free people to deal with. T hey can choose their own employers. No coercion is used to keep them on

the estates on which they are residing ; but on the contrary, in many instances advantages and inducements are held out to tho laborers to leave their original employ for another which is supposed to be more beneficial, and which in nine cases out of ten neither proves to be of any retnunerative results to the employer or cmplovcd. We would ask, what does all this tend to > To excite dissatisfaction and uneasiness to nine-tenths of our population, and to cause a bid feeling between neighbors, which as long as it exists must ultimately end in tho ruin of every one. We say this without hesitation, fur as sure as an estate is crippled by the want of labour, so sure are its neighbours destined to feel its influence. We know that the yearly contract is the mainstay of tho prosperity of the whole colony þÿ then why, with our eyes open, seek to destroy its goods effects by wilful corruption ? It is a slow poison, hut a poison that will prove fatal to all in the end. The most ultra-philanthropist to the labourer of | our colony must bo convinced of this, were he to weigh well all the advantages of the yearly contract with the reckless extravagance of daily labor. We see around us in tho neighbouring colonies, the population retrograding i-j civilisation, diverging to their aboriginal state and becoming careless of tho blessings that Providence has placed in their way. We have no doubt that our ideas on this subject will be criticised, they may even be scoffed at, but we earnestly

request our readers to reflect seriously on the consequences of a system as pernicious in its immediate effect as it will be ruinous in its ultimate results. Tho remedy is easy; fairness and candour among the Planters would check all the evils. We have no wish for any combination of employers, far from it ; wo wish to see tho labourer choose of his own free-will the Estato that he or she should select for their abode but ; wc do thoroughly condemn a practice of cajolery and bribery that every one knows, takes place more or less throughout the Island. We Lave heard some people try to justify their conduct by appealing to conscientious motives of doing the best for their employers interest. Bnt. this is a most shortsighted argument ; they forget that there is a future day, when those same employers will expect a return from their properties, and they even forget more. þÿ Do unto others, as you would they should do unto þÿyou. The very men who boast of conscientious motives to obtain

labour, forget that they are hurrying their neighbours and their own employers to an ultimate ruin which will eventually swallow up all the resources that a bountiful Nature has thrown open to our þÿindustry. i 1 ' Europe a n.

A private letter from Vienna says as follows : þÿ The Grand Puke Constantine himself now begins to despair of the cause of Russia, because she has to fight against invincible fleets and armies. þÿ Germany in the ensemble of its States, without excepting Prussia, thinks that Russia ought to renounce her projects of conquest, so that, though it loves Russia at heart, it will never take part against France and England, for in that case the wrath of those Powers would justly fall on Germany þÿalone. Another private letter from Vienna, says that the relations between the Allies and Austria have considerably changed for the better of late, and that the young Emperor recently declared to a diplomatic agent at the Court of Vienna that England and France had every reason to bo satisfied with the conduct of his Cabinet. That such a declaration was made by the Emperor I can assure you positively, but I fear that the sincerity of His Majesty, and the reality of the improvement in the relations in question, are not credited by many here. I ' u i n s of an Ancient California City þÿ Antiquarians will feel deeply interested in the discovery of vast regions of ancient ruins near San Diego, and within a þÿday s march of the Pacific Ocean, at the head of the Gulf ot California. Portions of Temples, dwellings, lofty stone pyramids, (seven of these within a mile square,) and massive granite rings or circular walls round venerable trees, columns and blocks of hierogliphics, all speak of some ancient race of men, now forever gone, their history actually unknown to any of the existing families of mankind. In some points, these ruins resemble the recently discovered cities of Palenque, See., near the Atlantic or Mexican coasts: in others again, the monuments of Phoenicia, and yet in many features they differ from all I have referred to. I observe that tliediscoverers deem them to lie antediluvian, while the present Indians have a tradition of a great civilized nation, which their ferocious forefathers utterly destroyed. The region of the ruins is called by the Imliars, the þÿ Valley of þÿMystery. þÿ IVilmer't Chronicle.

A pleasant anecdote is related of Partridge, who was celebrated for almanacmaking about one hundred years since. In travelling on horseback into the country, he stopped lor his dinner at an inn, and afterward called for his horse, that he might reach the next town, where he intended to sleep. As he was about to mount bis horse, the hostler said, þÿ If you will take my advice, sir, you will stay where you are for the night, as you will surely be overtaken by a pelting þÿrain. 11 Nonsense, þÿnonsense, exclaimed Partridge. þÿ There is a sixpence for you, my honest fellow, and a good afternoon to þÿyou. Partridge proceeded on his journey, and, sure enough, he was well drenched in a heavy shower. Partridge was struck by the þÿman p s rediction, and being always intent on the interests of bis almanac, lie rode hack on the instant, and was received by the hostler with a broad grin. þÿ Well, þÿsir, said he, þÿ you see I was þÿright. "Yes, my þÿlad, you have been so; and I will give you a crown on condition that you tell me how you knew of this þÿrain. þÿ Why, þÿsir, replied the man, þÿ the truth is, we have an almanac in our house, called þÿ Partridge s þÿAlmanac; and the fellow is such a notorious liar, that whenever he promises us a fine day, we always know that it will be the direct contrary.
