Selections. Irish Remittances. þÿ If the emigration drain from Ireland to the United States is being gradually diminished, as no doubt it is, the influx into Ireland of American money, earned by Irish hands, is steadily on the increase. Just take a few figures in illustration of this statement. The number who left Ireland for all parts of the States, British America, and Australia, in the year 1853, was 192,(509; whereas the number who left Ireland in the year 1854 did not exceed 150,209. Of these 1 1 1 ,095 emigrated to the United States, 22,999 to British America, and 16,203 to Australia. In 1853 the amount of money sent home by Irish emigrants to their relatives in Ireland, for payment of passages as well as for various other purposes, was £430,000; but in 1854 that amount, vast and wonderful as it was, was far exceeded, it having reached to £1,730,- 000, or nearly £.300,000 over what it was the previous year. In the history of the world there is nothing like this amazing proof of the strength and intensity of the feeling of affection and family attachment which has ever distinguished and adorned the calumniated Irish race. þÿ Cork Examiner.

THU DISTANCE OF I II 1. SUV Imagine a railway from here to the sun. How many hours is the sun from us? Why, if we were to send an infant in an express train, going a hundred miles an hour without making any stoppages, the infant would grow to be a boy, the boy would grow to be a man, the man would grow old and die without reaching the sun ; for it is distant, at this speed, more than a hundred years from us. But what is this compared to the distance of Neptune, one of the newlydiscovered planets? Suppose there had been a person who started, by a railway, at the creation of Adam and Eve, to go from Neptune to the sun, at the rate of fifty miles an hour, he would not have got there yet; for Neptune is more than six thousand years from our earth. What an idea does this give us of the extent of creation !

A LEVIATHAN STEAMER. In our paper of the 7th instant we noticed tinlaunch of the .splendid steam-ship Persia, as being the largest steamer in the world. Wc new read that there is positively being built at the Isle of Dogs (England) an iron steamer of 25.000 tons burthen. It is said in connection with this monster-ship that þÿ the wooden walls of Old England have given place to the iron-sides of Young Britain. Canvass has yielded the palm to steam ; and paddle-wheels in their turn are i shaking their bearings in auxiliary fear of þÿscrews. This huge fabric bears no resemblance to any known kind of craft. She is intended to make her first voyage to Australia. She will carry 12.000 tons of coals þÿ and space will still be left for 5,000 tons of cargo, and 4,000 passengers with their luggage, independent of the massive j machinery, and all necessary stores for use. Such is the Leviathan She is to he launched, unlike any other ship, broadside on to the water by means of hydraulic power, and early in next Spring is expected to make a trial trip to the United States and back in less than a fortnight.

America. The difficulty between the United States Go- i vernment and Fi ance, arising out of the arrest of J M. Dillon at San Francisco, is assuming rather a troublesome character, having recently formed the subject of a lengthy correspondence between Mr. Mason, the Minister at Paris, and Count VValewski, the French Minister of Foreign Affairs. The French Government, it seems, still insists upon satisfaction for the arrest of Mr. Consul Dillon, in the shape of a salute of a hundred guns in honour of his flag. The New York Herald states the circumstances that gave rise to this demand to be as follows : þÿ þÿ It will be recollected that when that dashing adventurer, the Count Raousset do Boulbon, meditated his expe- j dition into Sonora, for the purpose, in fact, of | planting a French colony there, and thus establishing a foothold for French interests in South America, he openly enlisted men in San Francisco for the military organisation which was to form its basis. In this it is charged that ho received, if not active aid, at least full countenance, from M. Dillon, the French Cousul at that port; Dillou himself, it is believed, acting cither under the instigation or direct orders of the French Minister iu Mexico. When preliminary steps were taken by the authorities at San Francisco to put a stop to these unlawful proceedings, it was found necessary to summon the French Consul before the tribunal charged with the investigation of the matter. M. Dillon refused to at-

tend, pleading that, by the consular treaty existing between the two countries, he was exempted from being called as a witness before the American courts. Judge Hoffman, before whom the question of exemption was argued, decided that the Constitution allowed no such rights to any foreigner, whatever might be his functions, and issued a warrant to compel the attendance of the Consul. M. Dillon was accordingly arrested and brought before the Judge; but, persisting in his refusal to give evidence, the matter was referred to the Government at Washington for its decision. In the meanwhile M. Dillou struck his flag, and wrote home to France a statement of the facts. Mr. Marcy, upon a review of the circumstances, decided that Judge Hoffman had exceeded his powers, and ordered the Consul to be set free. This did not, however, satisfy the French Government, which demanded in addition that a salute should be fired in honour of his flag. Mr. Secretary Marcy took shelter behind constitutional grounds. The reply of the French Government was that it had nothing to do with the American Constitution; that a treaty existed between the two countries which protected the persons of French agents from arrest; and that it had a right to demand redress for the violation of the conditions of that treaty. In this position the question has remained up to the present time. The French Government still insists upon its original demaud, and the object of the correspondence between Count Walewski and Mr.

Mason is to bring the matter to some immediate decision. The President, General Davis, and some other members of the Administration, are said to be opposed to any concession ; whilst Mr. Secretary Marcy is in favour of it, resting his opinion on the precedent established in the case of the Spanish Consul at New Orleans, when his house was sacked by a mob after the slaughter at Atarcs In that instance, orders were given by Mr. Webster that the þÿConsul s flag should be saluted when þÿrehoisted. A FIFTH POINT FOR RUSSIA. It is whispered in Government circles that the following scheme for an eventual settlement of the Eastern question is seriously under consideration : þÿ The cession of the Crimea by Russia to be made a fifth þÿpoint the Crimea to be restored to Turkey as a compensation for the Principalities, which would be annexed to Austria in consideration of Lombardy being given up to Piedmont. Thus Russia would be humbled and weakened, Turkey supported, Italy ameliorated, Austria contented, and France and England gloriously satisfied. The plan is at least bold and clever, and may be worth serious examination whenever our successes in the Crimea shall be such as to enable us to dictate to Russia. þÿ Tetter from Paris þÿ þÿ=s= GENERAL PICTON. I once heard an annecdote of Picton, from an officer, who was himself at Waterloo. Picton, I was told by this officer, was wounded the day before Waterloo, but had concealed his hurt, and with the most heroic fortitude remained in the field During the night, however, the

agony of his wound obliged him to send for a surgeon, who remained with him until dawn ; and, on his leaving, Picton thus addressed him : þÿ You say that my wound is dangerous þÿ mortal ; that I am unfit for duty, aud must be represented so the Duke þÿ? þÿ Such is my þÿopinion, said the medical man. þÿ I think it would be impossible for you to take command of y'our þÿdivision. þÿ Leave me to judge of that, þÿSir, said Picton, þÿ and in the meanwhile, allow me to ask you a question. From your long knowledge of me, do you consider me capable of strictly keeping my word þÿr þÿ I have every cause to believe þÿso, returned the surgeon ; þÿ but why the question, Sir The mas þÿ? þÿ Simply for this þÿreason, returned Picton, þÿ that I have made up my mind to be in the field with my brigade ; and 1 give you my word of honor, both as a gentleman and a soldier, that, if you place my name in your report as unfit for duty, 1 will shoot you with my own þÿhand. The surgeon shrugged his shoulders, shook Picton by the hand, and withdrew. The gallant þÿGeneral s name was accordingly omitted amongst the wounded ; and, as his wish had often been expressed, that he might die amidst the blaze of battle, he was gratified. REMARKS. ad $ 1 . What is ordered here is nothing more than a confirmation of the existing state of things. ad 2. The school-commission as well as the Inspector have on sundry occasions expressed their opinion that a dwelling for the teacher ought to be found at every school, and that only a few have been furnished with dwellings has been caused from pecuniary considerations, but this measure cannot he delayed any longer if school is to be kept in the afternoon as well as in the forenoon ; the classes being by this law reduced to contain only one half of the children, rooms for the teachers may probably at a trifling expense be arranged in the school-houses themselves. ad Chapter 2. This chapter corresponds with the first chapter of the present ordinance and the deviations from the same are indicated in the introduction to this draft. The following particulars may yet be noticed : The time of admittance is here (4) again fixed to what it was formerly twice yearly ; in the draft laid before the Colonial Council by Government the same was the case but the council made the alteration; the reasons given, viz: that there is only one yearly examination and that the most of the changes of abode take place in October appear to me to be of little consequence but the inconvenience that children on account of this alteration may be prevented entering school before they are nearly seven years old, and on the other hand kept in school till nearly 14 is so great that the law already has been infringed
upon, as the children are admitted at

any time during the year. The draft of the ordinance lor the danish schools in town did fix for the time of admissal twice a year, but this was altered by the home Government so that children may be admitted at all times in the preparatory class, which answers to the first class of the present draft ; the instruction in these classes is the same, therefore it would be of no inconvenience even to confirm what now takes place, admissal at all times. The hours of instruction are fixed in the forenoon to 8-1 1 J instead of 9-12 in the former regulations and 8-12 in the existing ones, for the reason that children on the more distant Estates have found difficulty in attending work at pro per hours in the afternoon. ad 10. The addition made to this corresponds with the contents of 20 of the ordinance of 6th September 1853. ad Chapter 4. The deviations from the corresponding Chapter 3 of the above named ordinance are in conformity with the principles laid down in the introduction. The following may furthermore be observed : The inconvenience occasioned by the admittance, dismissal and removal of the children being made dependent on the examinations at the same time the examinations were reduced to be only once a year, has already been noticed. In the same way this inconvenience as regards the admittance has been remedied in the 4th of this draft the 20th contains a direction concerning the removals twice a year from class to class. The permission to retain some of the children two years above the ordinary

age as monitors has not been renewed in the present draft. The inconvenience caused by this institution has partly been mentioned in the introduction; it may here be added that it seems unjust tow ; ards the parents to deprive them ot earning the money of the work of the children in order to having their services for nothing in school, and furthermore preventing those from the more distant Estates to attend work even in the afternoon on account of the separate instruction they are to receive after the ordinary school time ; vide ordinance 6th September 1853 18 efrn. 4. According to the directions of this draft at all events children cannot be kept back in the lower class as this would deprive them of the more complete instruction given in the upper class ; if the teachers even now that the classes have been reduced to about one half of the number of children cannot do without monitors, they will have to select them from among the children belonging to the class. ad 5 25. The superintendance of the countryschools has formerly been assigned to the Moravian llrethren and it is they who appoint the inspector and the teachers ; experience has shewn that this congregation has been unable to fulfill its duty, as teachers have not always been found for the schools, and those appointed had in several instances to be dismissed on account of incapacity or immoral conduct ; it has also happened that able teachers have been dismissed without regard to the wants of the schools. It appears proper that the
King should not bind himself to select the superintendance from among a particular creed especially as the instruction in religion is to be adapted to all creeds. St. Croix, June 1855. C. SARAFW.

It is well known that, ever since the change which took place in our social system some few years ago, and which rendered it necessary for the Government to enact laws and regulations suited to our altered circumstances, the observance of the stipulations which these laws enjoin, particularly as regards country labourers, have been each succeeding year more and more disregarded, until, in fact, their violation lias become in the conduct and estimation of many almost a matter scarcely necessary to cover or conceal, nay, so common have the evil practices here alluded to now become that there are some planters not ashamed, even in public, to justify and defend them. þÿAltho the regulations thus framed, in order to preserve the mutual interest of planters and labourers in their new relation to each other, are perhaps as good as could be reasonably expected under the circumstances which they emanated, yet it must be admitted they have defects which time and experience have made evident, but such as they are, few will have the hardihood to deny that, if judiciously and faithfully adhered to, a better state of things would not exist than the strife and confusion which at present prevail in some parts of the country, arising from the efforts made by managers and proprietors, not only to restrain their own from removing, but to entice away each þÿother labourers. s It would be unjust, however, not to admit that there are some planters,

who, much to their conform to the þÿ þÿRegulations, and, as far as in honor, endeavour strictly to their power, to allow the law to work fairly, and who are incapable of descending to such reprehensible proceedings : procedings which it may not, however, be surprising to hear are perpetrated, and exulted in, by ignorant and reckless men, indiffereut alike to their own character and to the general good of the Island, who, it is affirmed, often employ their machinations and corrupt influence for the base gratification of injuring or crippling their neighbours, but it is grievous to reflect that there are men of position and standing, aud supposed good sense, who it is feated are equally' culpable with those from whom, perhaps, better could not be expected, and who, after all, in some cases, may only be the instruments of others. These brief remarks are not intended for the purpose of attaching public odium to any one, were it so it would be needless, since those persons who are prominent in these matters are sufficiently notorious throughout the country, but they are made with an earnest desire to arouse public attention to the existence of an enormous evil which if not checked must produce the same disastrous effects here, as experience has shewn it has done elsewhere, and bring ultimate ruin on this Island, and it is also to be hoped, before too late, that the authorities will adopt such active measures as will compel more respect for the laws, and punish those delinquents who appear as

insensible to their own interest as they are to that of the colony in general. It may very naturally be argued that the remedy lor the abuses above hinted at rests with the planters themselves, if they will only abstain from them, and properly observe the laws, but this might be said with the same force of reasoning with regard to any other law instituted for the interest and good government of society which some men may choose to break ; bad men will always be found ready for their own selfish designs to violate the wisest and most wholesome rules that can be framed for their guidance and benefit, þÿ a course which once indulged in, spreads with impunity, until a crisis at length arrives, which, if not averted by the power and authority of those charged with the execution of the laws, must bring final ruin upon all þÿ the innocent as well as the guilty. The proverbial want of union among the planters of this Island, and their want of good faith in general one to another, makes it hopeless to expect that a remedy can be found for the evil complained of by virtue of any agreement amongst themselves, for, unfortunately, their combinations or pledges to each other for any purpose have no more durability or adhesion than a rope of sand, aud as a curious illustration of this fact, it is only necessary to refer

S ft. 9 1H D 1 £ ATI 3 to the subjoined copy of an agreement entered into recently by a number of planters and administrators, for the purpose therein set forth, which, strange as it may appear, was violated in more than one instance before it was a mouth old. It may not be out of place here to observe that a most fallacious, and, may be, a most fatal idea for their own interest, pervades the minds of some of our large proprietors þÿ videlicet, that by raising the price of labor so high as to render it impossible for the small or poor properties to compete with the large estates, sufficient labor would be thrown into the market for the advantage of the more productive ones, but if these silly people will only reflect they can easily convince themselves that labor will decrease on the very best properties in proportion to the number of smaller ones which may go out of sugar cultivation When a þÿman e s state is ruined for this purpose, it of course follows that he will turn it to the best advantage he can otherwise, and he will let or sell it in small parcels to squatters. V\ hat then, let me ask, will become of the tine estates ? Those who may wish to learn let them look at Demcrara, and there they can satisfy themselves as to the result which is sure to follow the system of out-bidding each other in the labor market, the consequence of which they will find is that nearly all the landed property in that colony is in the hands of those who formerly were labourers B J COPY. Local. þÿ We were apprehensive of a Hurricane on Saturday night. The Barometers fell several lines, causing much alarm to the þÿ Weaþÿther-wise, and the wind blew with all its fury, happily, however, steadily from the Southward, still tearing up trees and blowing down fences. According to þÿ þÿReed s Theory of þÿStorms we are led to the belief that this was but the remnant of a Gale, which we fear has done much damage to the Southern Islands. We shall be glad to learn otherwise. Whether virulent or otherwise, it behoves all parents to i have their children immediately vaccinated, that is to say those of them who have not already been The necessary precautions, we are told, are being adopted by the authorities to save our Island from that fearful Epidemic. -« v to- : þÿ Wreck. þÿ We learn that some portions of a wreck, together with a quantity of rum and sugar, were picked up at Sandy Point, West End, on Sunday last. Since we received the foregoing information our punctual correspondent at particulars. He says : þÿ Frederiksted has scut us the following additional þÿ 1 hasten to furnish you (for þÿTuesday p s aper) with the occurrences that have taken place here since my last regular communication. On the night of Saturday, the 25th, it blew a perfect gale ; towards morning the weather changed favorably, with a few intermediate showers þÿ it still blew freshly, however, during the whole of Sunday, which caused the sea to rise considerably. The Danish schooner St Croix, Capt. Way lington, and the sloop Eliza, Capt. George, stood firmly to their anchors and weathered out the gale. I am sorry, however, to inform you that a large vessel (name unknown) was stranded on the reef at the South

West point of this Island, and became a total wreck. Not a living being has been seen or heard of, therefore the presumption is that the parties belonging to the vessel either met with a watery grave or deserted in their boats. SIR WILLIAM MOLESWORTH. We have gieat pleasure in announcing that Sir William Molls wo ktii is to succeed Lord John Russell in the direction of the Colonial-office. We regard this appointment as among the first, and not the least valuable, fruits of the movement for Administrative Reform. There is no public man who has more fairly won his way to this distinction than Sir William Molesworth. It has been the habit to appoint men Colonial Secretaries because something must be done for them, because they were too intractable and troublesome to be trusted in any other department, because they were lazy, or because they were mischievously active for þÿ every reason in the world, in fact, except because they knew anything of the department they undertook to administer. To this time-honoured practice Sir William Moi.eswortii is a first and most signal exception ; he is a Colonial Secretary because he understands the colonies, and for no other reason whatever. It would be difficult to exaggerate the services which during his Parliamentary career the new Colonial Secretary has rendered to the cause of the colonies, and the degree in which, by so doing, he has consolidated and conciliated the remoter portions of this great empire. He was the first to denounce the intolerable evils resulting from the system of transportation to the Australian colonies, with ! to the monarch, who awarded þÿ
prosperity, and its moral rottenness. If not

3 IT « u till A 'T I 3, the founder, he may fuiily be termed the regenerator and purifier of that great group of dependencies. He was among the early colonizers of New Zealand, though entirely free from the questionable acts which afterwards discredited that noble undertaking. He possessed and imparted to Parliament vast stores of knowledge as to the complicated relations between the English settlers at the Cape of Good Hope, the Dutch Boer.s and the savage tribes by which they are menaced and surrounded. To him we mainly owe the establishment of the principle, now recognized as an axiom, but formerly ridiculed as a paradox, that to the colonies should be intrusted the management of their own affairs, and the establishment of that double electoral chamber, which seems likely to pervade all British communities, from Canada to New Zealand. To his untiring exertions we owe it that the country has been spared the enormous expense of maintaining troops in these distant regions and no one has thrown more light on the best constitution for and on the manner in which Imperial should be distinguished from local ! trate in that State has says powers. Extension of the Telegraph to India. þÿ The Turkish Government have granted an exclusive concession for a subinarino telegraph from the Dardanelles to Alexandria. The cost will be .£'120,000, and the line could be completed in twelve months. An annual subsidy of £4500 for twenty years is to be paid by Turkey for the transmission of official messages ; and, as the communications from India will be accelerated from five to six days when this and the general system of telegraphs now constructing in Eu- j ropean Turkey shall have been completed, an additional revenue of £10,400 is calculated upon by promoters the from that source. At the same time proposals are on foot for extending the project to India, by carrying the communication via Suez and Aden to Rurrachec, at the mouth of the Indus, where it would connect with the lines already in operation, or in course of construction, by the East India Company throughout the various presidencies. The total length from the Dardanelles to Kurrachee is about 4000 miles, and the mm required lor the whole (including the submarine line to Alexandria ) would be £850,000. Application has been made to the India-house for support, in the shape of an annual allowance of £30,000 a year, subject to reduction in proportion to the ultimate success of the undertaking. The entire line to India may, it is estimated, be completed in two years.

THE ISLANDS OF AVES We have been credibly iuformed that His Danish þÿMajesty sConsul-General at Venezuela has communicated officially to our Government that the Government of Venezuela has made known, in the public journals of the Republic, that the Aves or Bird Islands are to be considered as a portion of the national territory, aud consequently as being under the dominion of the Republic. The Consul-General is in possession of several decrees and circulars, from which it appears that the contract entered into on the 25th December, 1854, by the Venezuelan Government and J. D. T. Vallace, a citizen of the United States, granting a monopoly for the exportation of Guano from these Islands, has expired ; and that the Government inteuds to govern them in conformity with rules which are in course of being framed. As a result of this, all nations will be permitted to trade in Guano, not only from the Islands of Aves but also from other Islands under the dominion of the Republic, on which this article is to be found, on condition of subjecting themselves to certain regulations which will be alike for all, as well for foreigners as for natives. Until these regulations are made known, it is, however, not allowed that foreign vessels should engage in tho trade with Guano from these Islands without previously obtaining the permission of the Government of the Republic, and without paying the value of the export

THE WEATHER. j The Weather, which had assumed a threaten ing appearance during the days terminating the week, ended by blowing a perfect gale from the East the whole of Saturday night, the gusts at different periods being sufficiently severe to cause the apprehension that some of our buildings would be found injured in the morning. Happily no damage occurred to the town ; this must, however, be attributable to the precaution which our inhabitants manifest in securiug their dwellings during the Equinoctial term. The calamities which the Islanders have experienced in the past, has taught wisdom for the future, and measures are now taken to protect dwellings which in previous times were totally neglected ; as far therefore as human effort extends, buildings are now in a better condition to resist storms than they used to be The sea, in consequence of the severity of the wind, rose to an alarming height, which being slightly from the South, threw an immense swell against tho Wharfs, which are on the whole pretty well destroyed, aud will cost some heavy outlays to effect the necessary repairs. The destruction to the Wharfs is, however, now an almost annual occurrence, and ought, we should think, create a desire of combination with the Proprietors to adopt some general plan for constructing an entire Wharf along the business locality with a proper granite front. The outlay, at a first sigght, would no doubt seem startling, but if the years of expense for repairs, constant

new piles, þÿ4 C-> were taken in consideration, the measure in the end would prove an economical one þÿ to say nothing of the very many other advantages that would result from it. Lighters would then be no longer required, and vessels would come alongside and discharge their cargoes with ease aud despatch. To this we may add, that when we daily perceive the way in which the harbour towards the shore in filling up, tho project is doubly necessary, and not only is the attention of the Proprietors called, but that of the Government as well. Rather too much unconcern has been shewn on this very important ques tion, and deserves the bestowal of more energy and interest. Two English sloops the Rosabella, of Anguilla, and Louisa, of St Kitts, were unfortunately driven to the shore during the night, and as both were thrown to the same spot, the violence of tho waves caused them to injure each other a good deal. Their appearance in the morning was extremely discouraging, and it was supposed that unless taken off promptly, a further increase of the sea would tear them into fragments. It is our pleasing duty to mention that the Commander of the Spanish Steam-frigate Don Fernando el Catolico, yet lying in port, generously sent a Cutter, with a crew of twenty-five men, kedge, anchor, hawser, and other tackling, to their aid After a little skilful exertion and daring on the part of the sailors, the Louisa was safely hauled off. The weather continuing to abate, and tho day growing lato, no attempt was made on tho

other sloop I he following morning Captain Henry Johnson, of the Dutch schooner Alma, with tackling, cj'c., from the schooner, and the aid of a dozen shore men, undertook, without solicitation, and without charge, to set the Rosabella afloat, which was accomplished in the space of three or four hours. We cannot too loudly commend acts of such genuine good feeling, and to appreciate those who, in a moment of need, readily bestow their best efforts to relieve the misfortunes of others The Captains or Owners of the sloops were devoid of means to employ labour to save their vessels, and their sense of gratitude should be deep to the Commander of the Frigate, and to Captain Johnson þÿ St. Thomas Times, August 29.

The packet-schooner Vigilant, Captain Bo- | rer t Higgins, left our port at 6£ þÿo clock on Sunday morning for St. Thomas ; she arrived there at þÿnoon meeting the European steamer I at her moorings, as she had entered the harbor the day before (Saturday) while the Scholten was leaving it þÿ was detained there two hours, and returned here at 81 þÿo clock on Sunday night. The schooner could have been here earlier had she not been detained at St. Thomas, but this was unavoidable as she arrived during Divine Service, while the Post-office authorities were at Church, consequently the Mails were not immediately put on board. The packet, on her arrival here, was placed under quarantine. We cannot but admire and applaud the precaution used by our praise-worthy authorities to prevent the introduction, if possible, of any loathsome disease, whether epidemic or endemic, contagious or non-contagious, infected little Garden of the þÿWest. While þÿ into this hitherto dison the subject of epidemic diseases we may mention that we learn Small Pox has shewn its hideous shape at the Spanish Island of Porto Rico. The European intelligence by this mail is both important and interesting. Sweaborg (the second Gibraltar) has been destroyed by the combined fleets of tbe British and French ; Sebastopol, we learn, was also to be attacked by sea, and the bombardment was to be continued, if required, for twenty-one successive days. From this operation Sebastopol will and must fall A

foreign contemporary þÿ the Editor of the New head and truthfully asserts the following: þÿ York Courier and Enquirer þÿ þÿ Will Sebastopol be þÿCaptured, boldly writing under the þÿ As our table is literally loaded with communications upon the subject, we may as well, once for all, place on record our deliberate opinion, that nothing can prevent the rapture of Sebastopol by the Allies. If a million of men should become necessary, they must and will be furnished ; and the Crimea and Sebastopol must and will fall. Sebastopol will be taken, at whatever cost of men and money. It is no longer a matter of option with the Allies Necessity þÿ the preservation of the armies and the honor of England and France, alike demand its capture ; aud therefore all the resources of the two kingdoms must be expended before its capture can be abandoned þÿ We endorse this opinion. The Paris correspondent of the London Times, in reference to the fall of Sweaborg, remarks : þÿ þÿ The fortress of Sweaborg, which has just been bombarded by the Allied fleets, is built on granite isles, about a mile in advance of Helsingfors, the Russian capital of Finland, as Abo was formerly its Swedish capital. The isles in ques tion, eight in number, are mere rocks connected together by a strong fortification, and in the centre is situate the part where the Russian flotilla is kept. The largest of the rocks is that called þÿ Gustavus þÿSword, on which is built the resi-

dence of the Governor, with a sort of garden formed of mould brought from the main land, and a vast cistern, in which is heaped together a large quantity of snow in winter to furnish water to the garrison. Swenborg has been called the Gibraltar of the North ; it would seem, however, not with as much justice as was formerly thought, since the late bombardment shows it to be anything but impregnable. The islands flank each other, and all have the granite cut perpendicularly to a height of from 30 to 40 feet. The only passage by which the roadstead of Helsingfors, which is one of the great war ports of Russia, can be reached winds along these formidable isles, which are armed with 800 guns of large calibre. As Sweaborg only presents an unapproachable reinture of granite, a siege of it could not be made by land, aud tbe place could only bo reduced by a famine. But it might be attacked and demolished from tbe sea by means of a bombardment, and this is what has just been executed with full success by the Anglo-French fleet, a bombardment which must have caused immense material losses to the Russian Government, by destroying the barracks, the different maritime establishments, aud the arsenal of the fort. Sweaborg was constructed in the 18th cen- I tury by the King of Sweden, Gustavus III. In the revolution which dethroned Gustavus IV, in 1808, and which afforded Russia the long sought opportunity for invading Finland, the impregnable fortress was given up without resistance to

the Russian General Barclay de Tolly, by a traitor who forgot what was due to his country iu gratifying his political passions. Sweaborg has a population of about 3,400 persons. Its barracks can hold more than 12,000 men ; and, besides its fine port, it has two basins to repair þÿships. The works of the Allies against Sebastopol are, as General Felissier reports, pushed on actively on all points, and tho besieged has made no new attempt to impede them The Russians attacked the French works on the Malakoff side on tho night between the 24th and 25th July, but with no better success than the former attack. Letters from the ('riinoa state : þÿ General þÿI elissier will not trust anything to chance, and though for the most part our approaches are close to the place, orders are given to push them closer still. The greatest confidence of our success appears to exist, and though there is nothing official in the news, it is generally thought that the fire of the new batteries will open on the 16th (August), the anniversary of the þÿEmperor fete. s Our batteries are truly formidable ; they have been constructed with the greatest care, and with strict regard to all the rules of military science. The Moniteur says--- The brilliant successes of the Allied fleets in the Baltic will, we confidently trust, be strongly followed by a not less complete triumph of the brave army now besieging Sebastopol. The Vienna Military Gazette considers as certain and immediate the success of our attack upon the place. Our approaches are so close
to the þÿenemy l s ines that on some points they almost touch them, so that the struggle cannot be long delayed. We may accordingly soon expect to hear of some important event.

By t he arrival of the Carmei from Constantinople we have full details of the battle fought en the Tchcruaya on the Ifith. Encouraged, it may be, by tlie arrival of a portion of the Grenadiers, and probably urged on by the impatience ol high personages at St. Petersburg, the Russian General determined on an attack on the allied position, and made preparations for many days, with a disregard of caution which revealed his plans and, but for extraordinary remissness, should have caused their more easy discomfiture. It is said that the movements of the Russian force were plainly visible þÿ that their collections ot pontoons and engineering materials were exposed in front of their position, and that no means were taken to hide the proximity and the magnitude ol' the attack from a foe whom the Muscovite General might have learnt to respect, hut whom the oft repeated alarms of an attack had lulled into security. At last, on the morning of the 10th the Russians, pouring down the steep sides of their position and favoured by the mist, without cry or beat of drum, burst upon the Piedmontcse position : driving in the outposts, they reached the Tchernaya, forded the narrow stream, and, notwithstanding a heavy fusillade from the Zouaves, rushed upon the allied camp. They attacked two French regiments in front and flank with a desperate bayonet charge, and a hot contest ensued, in which General D'Hkrbili.ON, with 10,000 men, had to sustain the attack of the Russians, who probably by
this time had brought a much larger force into

action, Reinforcements, however, soon arrived, and a long and formidable combat ensued, in which the Russians wore beaten on every point. Their artillery was silenced by the superiority of the allied fire, and they appear to have been on this occasion entirely outdone in the effective management of their favourite arm. Their greatest loss, no doubt, was from the deadly action of the enemy's cannon and rifles against their advancing columns. Descending a slope, they presented the fairest aim lor the well-served artillery of an enemy, and the Minie and curabine-a-tige, with which the French are armed, must have done deadly execution upon them before they could reply with their inferior weapons, or close, as they appear to have attempted, in hand-to-hand combat. The superiority of position as well as of military skill on the part of the allies is proved by the great disproportion of loss on the two sides. While the Russians are officially declared to have suffered to the extent of 6,000 men, probably a fifth of those actually engaged, the French and Sardinians together compute their loss at only 1,200 men. No less than 900 prisoners had arrived at Constantinople when the packet left. No attempt was made to follow up the victory, and indeed such an enterprise would have been impossible. General Pelissier says tliat General Mouius, who commanded the cavalry, was eager to pursue the enemy, but his own opinion was that enough had been done, and the judgment of the Commander-in-Chief must command assent.

In a country so difficult as the Crimea the attacking party has always the disadvantage ; and, though the defeated and retreating Russians might have suffered from a charge of cavalry, it is difficult to say that some such fate as that of Ralaklava might not have awaited the adventurous General, had he advanced far into a tract of land where cavalry might easily be placed in a difficult position, and when the enemy possess the advantage of a superior knowledge of the ground. As for an advance against the Russian position itself, that is a matter for the most cautious strategy, and not for soldiers with blood roused by the excitement of a new victory. The day went sufficiently against tho Russians, whom it foiled in a long-planned scheme and roused from a dream of success, which we may think absurd, but which we see was sufficient to lead thoin on to immense exertions and a most hazardous and deadly conflict. It is not, difficult to see the object ol the Russian General, though how he could hope for success is sufficiently surprising. G oim se n \ koff knew that the allies were pressing close their works round tho Malakoff ; that the batteries they were erecting were on a scale and of a power unknown in the past history of the siege ; that, in spite of sorties and ambuscades, his soldiets had never rcgaiued a foot of ground that 'hey had lost ; he know that the ships and the steamers in Sebastopol were in danger, and that even tho daily communication with the north side ot the harbour might soon be threatened.

It, was expedient, then, to seize a position from which he could annoy the allies, menace a continual and advantageous attack, and divert them from the assault of the Malakoff, or force then, to attempt it with diminished forces while the flower of their army should bo watching the Tchcrnaya. It was a bold idea, and the means taken to carry it out wore probably correct enough according to the rules of war. Rut the Russian Generals forget one thing, or, with negligent cruelty to those they lead, disregard it where the faintest hope of success appears. They have yet to learn or more thoroughly appreciate the inferiority of their troops in the open field. 1 he late Czar could not, it is said, believe it, yet probably a conviction of its truth reached his

3 1T © Hi 0 1 X A T I 3. heart sufficient to embitter his latter days. Behind the works which they have constructed with such labour and such enduring courage they have fought with success, and may still further prolong resistance, but until the social causes which form the character of the soldier be changed he will never, especially in offensive operations, equal those against whom he is now engaged in conflict. There is one point which must gratify all readers of this brilliant victory. The Sardinians, fiercely attacked, fought with desperation, and in the long struggle which followed showed themselves worthy comrades of the French and British. Piedmontese valour had till this eventful day no means of showing that its flame had not become dim since the times of its former glory. The troops of \ ictor Emmanuel had arrived late on the scene. The officers, a noble and high-minded class ot men, had, perhaps not unnaturally, been surprised and mortified by the apathetic reception given to them by the Turks, ignorant that the 1' reuch and British had long before wondered at the same obtuseness, although they regarded it too little to take ortonce. lu the Crimea there was nothing for them to do. They encamped in the valley which has been lately the scene of their heroism. Either through some agreement, or through the unwillingness of tho French and British to have foreign troops in their lines, they were excluded from the trenches. Then came sickness, which decimated their force. They were much discouraged, and began to murmur.

A political party at home, which had opposed their being seut at all, began to exult in the accomplishment of its gloomy prophecies. One day has suffered to change the spirit of the Piedmontese. 1 hey are brothers in arms to tho allies, who had before met the enemy; they can be content to wait for further renown until operations are attempted in which they can have a share. They have justified their claim to high consideration on the part of the world, aud vindicated the wisdom of the Government which sent them to fight for civilization that they might be a source of hope and confidence to unhappy Italy until the day arrives for her deliverance. A very sanguinary affair occurred oil the 17th July at Gambia, the natives having broken out in open rebellion in consequence of an attempt to arrest a man who had carried away a man and his wife from a village for slaves. The police and small military force were repulsed. Lieut. Armstrong was wounded, and two soldiers were made prisoners. The marauders then burned three English villages, on which Governor O'Connor proceeded with 260 men to take St. Mary's, but was waylaid by the natives, and driven back with a loss of 30 killed and 43 wounded. Among the latter was Governor O'Connor. He then obtained the assistance of a f ronch þÿMan þÿof \\ ar, and 150 white troops, who carried the town at the point of the bayonet, and on the 3rd totally destroyed it. The French had 2 killed and 5 wounded. The British bad none killed, but 30 with volunteers wounded. The natives lost above 200. Uathurst is in a very insecure state.

Exchange of Colonial Dependencies with France. þÿ The Paris Presse has the following on the talked of exchange between France and England of certain colonial dependencies: þÿ "The English papers have lately spoken of the intended purchase by France of the Islands of Dominica and St. Lucia, English colonies in the Antilles, in exchange for Chundernngor, a French possession in Bengal. This account is not exactly correct. The matter in question appears to be the reciprocal cession of some French and English possessions held by the two Powers in the East Indies. France was the first to make a proposition on this subject, and it has, it is said, been favourably received. France has five settlements in India, at considerable distances from each other: Chandernagor, at the bottom of the Bay of Bengal; Kankal, Malic, Tanaon, and Pondicberry. Each of these establishments, within a restricted space, has English settlements between them, and they are sources of embarrassment for both countries. The object, therefore, will be to form a kind of contiguity in the settlements of the respective countries by mutual exchange."

A Boy with a Real þÿTail At Middlesho rough-on -Tees there exists a singular freak ot nature, " a boy with a real tail He is about four months old and in good health. He has a perfect caudal appendage four or five inches in length, It springs from the vertebrae of the os sacrum, not the os coccygis, as does the tail of an animal, which is a continuation of the spinal structure. It has caused much interest among the faculty, who have had a consultation whether it would be proper to take it off"; but, as upon examination it is found to possess the properties of a limb, having bone, muscle, feeling, &,c., and can be moved at the will of the child, it is feared the operation might endanger the child's life by affecting the spinal cord. A Cholera Incident. þÿ A curious circumstance is stated to have occurred in the Mendicant's Asylum of the Monte Domini at Florence :þÿ The cholera recently attacked some of the residents, and it increased rapidly, to the great terror of everybody in the place. All at once, the director, in order to raise the courage of the persons under bis charge, announced that the malady had ceased, and that it was his intention to give a grand fete to celebrate its departure, lie, in consequence, gave a theatrical performance, and a dance, and made all the mendicants partake of an excellent supper. All this created such a favourable impression upon the men's minds, that the next day not a single new ease of cholera occurred, adding another proof to the many already in existence of the powerful effect of the state of mind in times of cholera invasion.

THE LATE M. DE D1ELKE Diplomatists are birds of passage. Here today and there to-morrow, they settle on our shores for a brief space, and then wing their flight to other lands. Their stay among us is generally so short, and their habits are usually so migratory andreseived, that it is only as rare exceptions that they leave behind them anything more than a mero recollection of their visit. One calls to mind for a while the fine clothes of

the great man as he made his appearance at the þÿQueen s Drawing-room, or shone in the Diplomatic Tribune in the House of Lords, but after he has fluttered out his brief existence here, and so fulfilled his mission, nothing remains but the remembrance of the wondrous plumage of the rare bird. So it is with diplomatists in the mass, but it is not so with the man whose name stands at the head of this notice. There have been, of course, other exceptions to the general rule just laid down ; the mind and feelings of the reader will reudily supply them, but in none does | the exception more forcibly prove the rule than in the case of the late AI. de Bielke. Sprung of one of the most noble families of the north þÿ a family noble, not by the accident of birth alone, but by the long list of its worthies who have adorned the annals of the sister kingdoms of Denmark and Sweden þÿ M. de Bielke early devoted himself to diplomacy, and after a successful career was promoted to be Secretary of Legation to the Danish Alission in this country. In ordinary times such a post may be filled equally well by almost any one ; where there is little to do a little man will do it as well as one of greater proportions; but thelatter portion of M. de þÿBielke s stay in this country was no ordinary time ; there was work to be done, and Denmark was fortunate iu having at the Court of St. þÿJames a s diplomatist equal to the occasion. In the year 1S48 the crash of a falling throne in France had awakened German patriotism from its trance.

To the cold torpor of despotism succeeded the hot fit of a freedom which know not how to be free. All Germany was revoluti jnized, and on her northern frontier a mob of mad enthusiasts, urged on by iiisaue professors, and patted on the back by the now reactionary King of Prussia, threw themselves across the Evdcr j,U(j jDvart, þÿ the dq-;-;ons of the Xing Denmark. The 0f embers of that insurrection are now extinct, þÿ even as the fire among the þÿthorns, and Germany has relapsed into her despotic Slough of Despond, leaving þÿ Sehleswig-IIolstein oceanþÿgirdled to its fate ; but at the moment the blaze was hot and the emergency great Denmark was poor and weak ; Schleswig-Holstein was powerful, with all Germany at its back. While the Danes, with hereditary daring, prepared to receive and repel the invaders at home, the temper aud ingenuity of their diplomatic agents abroad were taxed to the uttermost to expose the fallacies and combat the specious subtleties of the Schleswig-Holstein emissaries. In this war of words aud strife of notes and protocols þÿ in this assiduous sap and countersap and mine and countermine, directed now against this or that diplomatist, now agiinst the Foreign-office þÿ none played a more distinguished part and rendered his country more signal service than Rodolph de Bielke. Nor was his time entirely spent in the tortuous approaches of Downingstreet, or wasted in the tnole-like operations of a diplomacy which works always underground and succeeds best when it is most concealed. He

early appreciated the advantage of publicity, and felt that his þÿcountry cause s could stand the light of day. By his means the great organs of public opinion in England were gradually enlightened as to the relative positions and rights of the contending parties in Denmark, and it is to bis indefatigable efforts, more than to those of any other man, that Denmark owes the formation of a saner judgment in England on the merits of the Schleswig-Holstein quarrel, the intricacies of which, increased by the devices of the enemies of Denmark, at one time threatened to weary the patience of Europe. Unlike most men who have deserved well of tbeir country, M. de Bielke had the rare good fortune of being appreciated at Copenhagen His merits were recognized and rewarded, first,
on the lamented decease of Count Reventlow, who had been his diplomatic chief, by b ii)» ap-

post of Danish Minister at Berlin. He had lived so long among us, and was so thoroughly one of us, that we parted from him, as if the separation was only to be short, and we reckoned on his speedy return. The fulfilment of that hope has been denied us by the decree of Providence. Of almost gigantic stature and Herculean frame, liodolph de Bielke seemed the last man likely to be cut off in the prime of life. But an ill-advised visit to a German bath þÿ an imprudent recourse for a sjrall cause to those melancholy waters which have washed out the vigour of so many manly frames þÿ sent him back to Berlin with a constitution wasted aud worn out, and ultimately forced him to seek across tne Alps the health which he had lost in Germany. This object was only partially attained, and our friend was on his way home when he was seized with cholera, at Padua, and, though he succeeded in shaking off the immediate attack, it left him so weak that his enfeebled frame was unable to prolong the struggle for life which had already lasted so many months. He expired at Padua on the 26th of July, leaving behind him the memory of a man brave as a lion yet gentle as a child, firm as the granite of his native North and true of temper as her steel. If his countrymen should exclaim on hearing of his loss, þÿ Denmark has many such among her þÿsons, we can only reply, Denmark is fortunate in having so large a storv of native worth. In other countries characters like Kodolph de Bielke come few and far
between. þÿ London Times, August 14 THE BATTLE ON THE TCHERNAYA.

Admiral Bruat has addressed a letter of some length and of great value to the French Government, iu which he gives his opinion of the effect of the battle of the Tschernaya upon the Russian army, and also states that if the Allied Powers exhibit a little more patience, that Russia must relinquish her hold at Sebastopol before the close of the forthcoming winter. The Admiral says : þÿ No engagement had ever before proved in so striking a manner the superiority and moral ascendancy of our troops over those of the enemy. The arrangements made by the Russian army indicate a we'.l-concerted and well-studied plan. No error similar to that of General Soimonoff at the battle of Inkcrmann was committed on this day. The Russian divisions attacked our positions at the prescribed hour, and with a perfect knowledge of the ground ; they took possession of the bridge of Traktir, and forced the Sardinian advanced posts to fall back When the brigade of General de l'ailly assumed the offensive, 1,500 or 2,000 Frenchmen drove back 8,000 Russians beyond the Tchernaya, and in an hour after 45,000 Russians retreated before 10,000 or 12,000 of the allied troops. The affair of the 16th was much less a battle than an immense sortie, repulsed with incredible vigour. The enemy had not advanced out of reach of his heavy batteries, and he retired under the protection of the works which crown the plateau of Mackenzie as soon as he perceived that our troops were not intimidated by the considerable masses which he had deployed

He had, perhaps, hoped to draw us under the fire of his heavy batteries, and to get our troops among the heights, whence his artillory could have played upon us with destructive effect. By bringing forward his cavalry he might have made a few prisoners, but our squadrons must have passed over the bridge of Traktir, which

SUGAR MANUFACTURE. (From The Journal of the Society of Arts, July 13.) Sir, þÿ I address you with a twofold object; firstly, to give a short account of improvements in sugar mills, manufacture «fcc. ; secondly, to try and receive through your columns information relative to the growth of sugar up the Nile. Sugar mill rollers were formerly made to revolve from 5 to 7 revolutions in a minute. Now it is found that three or four revolutions allow the cane-juice to drop away more clearly and fully, and that the niegass, or refuse cane, is consequently so much more easily dried, and becomes better fuel. Such colonies as Trinidad and Demerara have long suffered from want of proper fuel. W. llurnley Hume, Esq., (second son of the deceased M. P.), informs me that cane, which was underground drained in 1845- 9-7, is now giving a most unparalleled return of fine sugar. He is also an ad-

3 U>» ATIS vocate for good high chimnies at sugar works, and railways for the colonies. No fairer field presents itself to intelligent sober engineers, than the colonies of Demerara and Trinidad, for the erection of saw mills. Can you kindly give me any information relative to the growth of sugar up the Valley of the Nile? I fear to trespass further on your valuable space. Yours, &e., Mackenzie Dick. 23, Newman-street, London, June 1855. P.S. þÿ Having acted as one of two judges at the ploughing match ever held in the fine island of Trinidad, in 184G, 1 feel an interest in the welfare of the colony, which is comparatively in a virgin state, abounding in fine timber and rich lands. Certainly, the Americans are more apt to run light saw mills (water or steam) than the Britishers. Something in the shape of Dr. Arnott's ventilators would, I think, be of use in evaporating chambers, both at home and abroad þÿ of course on a large scale.

The French Press on Lord Raglan. þÿ The Paris Union, in the course of a short article, has the following fair appreciation of the character and services of the lamented Lord Raglan : þÿ " Calm and resolute in action, more imperturbable in execution than prompt to conceive and be moved, of a constancy which nothing could tire out, he comprised in himself that cool bravery, that intrepid firmness, but slow, which are the principal qualities of the English soldier. To these he joined the elegant bravery, the mental adornment, the elevation of character which distinguish the British aristocracy. The marvels of Valour accomplished by our troops inspired him with a sincere admiration, and he appreciated the concurrence, often salutary and decisive, which our columns afforded to bis battalions. One day, after one of these auxiliary arrivals so opportunely in aid, he exclaimed, ' The French have taken away one of my arms at Waterloo, they come to restore it to me.' Lord Raglan suffered deeply from the disasters which afflicted his army, and if English usages did not associate him so directly with the sufferings of the soldier, as is the case with us þÿ if he was not, without ceasing, like our generals, mixed with the daily life, with the anxieties, the joys, and the sufferings of the troops þÿ he had a deep interest for bis own. The homage which we render to one of the bravest sons of England possesses even from our impartiality a character which will distinguish it from others."

THE WONDERS OF PHOTOGRAPHY. Recently at the Polytechnic Institution, Paris, a curious illustration was i given of the capabilities of photography in experienced hands. Two photographs were exhibited, one of the largest, and the other the smallest, ever produced by this process. The first was a portrait the full size of life, and the last was a copy of the front sheet of the London Times on a surface scarcely exceeding two inches by three ; both pictures were exceedingly perfect. The portrait, it is said, being more pleasing

and far more correct than those usually produced while the copy, notwithstanding its exceeding minuteness, could be read without the assistance of a magnifying glass. The capabilities of this comparatively new and exceedingly interesting art are just beginning to be experienced. Indeed, few outside of the class which make photography a specialty are aware of the diversified use to which it can be put. Mr. Gurney, whose Daguerrean and Photographic saloons are at 349 Broadway, has succeeded in obtaining full length portraits on canvas by it, which excei in the estimation of many, the best efforts of the pencil. þÿ New York Herald.

THE BRITISH ARMY. The total Army Establishment of Great Britain on the 1st of June consisted of twenty-five regiments of horse of various denominations, and one hundred regiments of toot, besides colonial and irregular troops and militia. Victory ! Victory ! ! Victory ! ! I The first day of October, 1855, was marked here by an event which absorbs all others, namely, the tidings of THR FALL OF SEBASTOPOL ! The schooner Vigilant arrived here on Monday morning, conveying the j above startling intelligence ; the mails were brought out to St. Thomas by

the Royal Mail þÿCompany f s ar-famed Litt Plata. \X e have before us the London Times , Mon ing Chronicle and Weekly Dispatch , of the latent dates, with full particulars of the glorious victory o! the Allies, and memorable defeat of the Russians. Our little Islat d resounds with the echo of þÿ Sebastopol is þÿtaken. The mind cannot picture the exultation that must have prevailed throughout England and France on receipt of the news of the fall of that Russian stronghold. One writer says: þÿ þÿ London w;.s fairly thrown off its balance by the announcement of the triumphant issue of the dread struggle. For a time the rush of the multitude to obtain early copies of the evening journals bore a strong similitude to an emeute. 'Fite excitement spread rapidly through all the crowded streets. From every church tower and stecplo the bells ran/ out the alarum of victory with deafening clamour. The French embassy was the first to illuminate. The tli ree sides of the house were brilliantly lighted, and around each of the windows in the front was fixed a large design, 30 feet square, with the French and English crowns, the flags of each nation, and the letters N and E, V and A, surrounded by immense laurels. There were also the letters composing the word þÿ þÿSebastopol, in red, white, and blue, the illumination consisting altogether 10,000 lamps. of þÿ At the several theatres the announcement from the stage was received with immense enthusiasm, in so < o cases producing an almost

electric effect. þÿ Next morning, the customary salutes of 4 1 guns were fired from the Tower and Park guns. The docks presented a most animated appearance, vessels ol all nations dressing ship with flags from the truck to th-: þÿwater s edge, the royal standard of Briiain floated proudly from the Tower, Somerset-house, the Adrniralty, and the Royal parish churches, and the hells in the metropolis sent forth merry þÿpea's.

On the 8th of September at noon, the signal for the assault was given A few moments afterwards the Allies were masters of the Malakoff, and at dusk the Russians, despairing of continuing a resistance in the other defences of the place, abandoned them at the same time, and hastily evacuated Sebastopol.

The following Despatch, dated September 10, has been received from General Pelissier : þÿ þÿ I inspected to-day Sebastopol and its lines of defence. The mind cannot have an idea or exact picture of our victory, the full extent of which can only be understood by an inspection of the place itself. The multiplicity of the works of defence and the material means applied thereto exceeding by far anything hitherto seen in the history of war. The capture of the Malakoff. which compelled the enemy to fly, has placed in the hands of the Allies an amount of materiel and

immense establishments, the importance of which it is not yet possible to state exactly. Tomorrow the Allied Troops will occupy the Karabelnaia aud the town, and under their protection an Anglo-Fenah Commission will be occupied with making out a return of the materiel abandoned \ to us by the þÿenemy.

General Pelissier has been created a Marshal of the Empire ! For the success of the Allies, the Emperor of the French has caused Solemn Thanksgiving to be rendered to Almighty God, who disposes of the fate of armies. On Sunday, the 16th September, a Te Deum was sung in all the departments of the Empire. It is stated that there was a mutiny among the Russian soldiers in Sebastopol on the 28th Aug., and on the following day 100 men were shot for their contumacy.

E X G LAN D. þÿ Public Excitement. þÿ On Monday evening, the 10th September, the most intense and enthusiastic excitement prevailed throughout the Metropolis and its suburbs in consequence of the news of the Fall of Sebastopol. About 9 þÿo clock the guns in St. þÿJames s Park, as well as those at the Tower, thundered forth their notes of victory, and the bells at many of the principal churches rung out their joyous peals ; while in the many of the main thoroughlures groups of people might be seen standing round one reading the despatches by light of gas. At St. þÿGeorge ( s and probably at other) barracks the troops were made acquainted with the glorious successes obtained by their brothers in arms, at the þÿ þÿroll-call, at nine þÿo clock, and the fifes and drums struck up in their fullest power þÿ God save the þÿQueen and þÿ Partant pour la þÿSyrie. At the Haymarket Theatre, Mr. Buckstone came on the stage between the acts, paper in hand, and read the despatches which had been received The audience rose en masse, cheering the intelligence to the echo, and when the orchestra performed þÿ God save the þÿQueen and þÿ See the Conquering Hero þÿcomes, very building vibrated from the tempest of applause .

ARMISTICE AND CAPITULATION. The Paris correspondent of the London Daily News þÿsays I have received from a good private source some interesting intelligence regarding the present state of things in the Crimea It will have been remarked that one of General Pelisþÿsier despatches, s while stating that Prince Gortschakoff had asked for an armistice to bury his dead left behind near Fort St. Paul, does not say whether or not he had acceded to the request It is certain that the French General felt it his duty to refuse, and I believe his very proper answer was, that he would bury the Russian dead himself, and would take the same care of their wounded as he did of hisown. General Pelissier has, I understand, telegraphed for instructions in case Prince Gortschakoff should offer to capitulate, an event which he thinks exceedingly probable, seeing that the Russian army is believed to have but fifteen þÿdays provisions, and to be very short of ammunition. An answer worthy ot the Allied Powers has been sent by the Emperor to his General, and this I am told is the substance of it : þÿ þÿ Our conditions arc that the Russians must surrender at discretion, lay down their arms, and give up to the Allies all the fortified daces in the Crimea, including Odessa, with all the munitions of war contained in them, and without any damage being previously done either to the towns or the fortifications."

The Paris correspondent of the Morning Post writes þÿ þÿ I am glad to see that the leading journals of the English press are alive to the necessity of completing the destruction of Russia. The sacrifices which England aud France have already made are too great fo be thrown away on any paper promises which Austria may bring forward in the name of Russia. The Emperor of the French has built his throne on the will of the people Queen Victoria reigns by the love of the nation, and by right. Both Sovereigns are surrounded by faithful aud patriotic þÿadvisers.

To sum up tho Russian loss, we may state that all the bastions, earthworks and granite forts, South of the great harbour þÿ Malakoff, Great and Little Redan, Flagstaff, Central Tower and Quarantine battery þÿ the sea defences, Forts Alexander, St. Nicholas and St. Paul ; the second line defence, the Garden and Barrack batteries, the Dockyard, Harbour and Careening Bay, with the full cannon sweep of Sebastopol roads þÿ all are in the power of the allies. The Russian Black Sea fleet has perished utterly. How many war ships have been sunk and how many burned we must wait to know, and it matters little, for all have been destroyed. The language of the Generals and Admirals is explicit ; not one of the proud ships of Sinope could now be found to carry a Mentschikoff to Constantinople.

The entire South side of the harbour of Sebastopol is in the possession ol the allies þÿ not a single Russian remains there except as a prisoner. To enable our readers to form as clear a conception ol the process by which this important issue has been obtained, as the telegraphic dispatches admit ol, we submit to them a resume of the operations from the moment of reopening the bombardment. The French and English batteries opened their fire at daybreak on the 5th inst. The bombardment was continued all that day and the next without slackening. On the night between the 5th and (5th, a Russian two-decker was set on fire by a shell, and burnt to the water-edge.
